docs.title: Field notes
docs.text:
The real process behind these items — what they are, how they were used, and why they matter. Tap to expand.

attitude control array

Reaction wheels or CMGs for precise spacecraft orientation without propellant expenditure.

A set of spinning flywheels (reaction wheels) or control moment gyroscopes (CMGs) that exchange angular momentum with the spacecraft to rotate it without firing thrusters. Enables precise pointing of instruments, solar panels, and antennas.

Real-world use · The ISS uses four control moment gyroscopes to maintain attitude, saving significant propellant. The Hubble Space Telescope uses reaction wheels for arcsecond-level pointing precision. CMGs are more power-efficient than thrusters for continuous attitude maintenance and are standard on all large spacecraft.

  • When · First use on OSO-1 (1962); widespread use throughout the space age.
  • Where · On all spacecraft requiring controlled attitude — from CubeSats to space stations.

Why it matters · Attitude control without propellant expenditure is an elegant engineering solution: use stored angular momentum to rotate the spacecraft, then periodically desaturate using thrusters when the wheels are spinning near maximum speed. This is the space equivalent of the flywheel in a steam engine — a mechanical store of rotational energy that smooths out variations. The flywheel appeared in T2; the attitude control array is its T6 descendant. In Conduvia, proper attitude control is required for rendezvous, solar panel orientation, and instrument operation.

basic comms satellite

First-generation communications relay satellite — enables over-the-horizon contact.

A basic geostationary or low-Earth-orbit communications relay satellite carrying S-band and X-band transponders. Receives signals from one ground station and retransmits them to another, enabling contact between surface locations with no line-of-sight.

Real-world use · Telstar 1 (1962) was the first active communications satellite; Syncom 3 (1964) the first geostationary comms satellite. Today's GEO comms satellites carry hundreds of transponders covering vast geographic areas. LEO constellations (Starlink, OneWeb) use many smaller satellites to provide global broadband.

  • When · 1962 (Telstar) onward; mass deployment of LEO constellations 2019–present.
  • Where · LEO (200–2000 km altitude) for low-latency coverage; GEO (35 786 km) for hemispheric coverage with three spacecraft.

Why it matters · A single comms satellite enables reliable contact between any two points that can see it — a capability that took surface relay towers, cables, or ship messengers previously. In network terms: one satellite links every surface node with clear sky access to every other such node, replacing N² direct connections with N connections to one hub. This is the T6 version of the same connectivity principle introduced in T0 by waypoints and camp markers — but now the reach spans a planet.

basic launch pad complex

Ground support infrastructure for a small orbital launcher.

A launch pad complex including a launch mount, propellant loading lines, flame trench and deflector, umbilical tower, and basic blast-resistant service structures. Designed to support one launch configuration at a time.

Real-world use · Launch pads are expensive, specialised infrastructure. The flame trench redirects combustion gases to prevent structural damage on ignition. The flame deluge system quenches engine exhaust and suppresses acoustic damage. Umbilical lines supply propellant, pressurisation, and power to the vehicle until milliseconds before launch.

  • When · 1950s onward with modern launch complexes.
  • Where · Coastal or inland sites with clear airspace, preferably at low latitudes to maximise rotational velocity contribution to orbital energy.

Why it matters · The launch pad is infrastructure, not a product — it does not go to orbit. It is the prerequisite for everything that does. This is a pattern repeated throughout Conduvia: kilns make ceramics but stay on the ground; bloomeries make iron but don't move; launch pads support spacecraft but are not spacecraft. Infrastructure cost is real. The launch pad requires significant resources to build, and its capabilities directly constrain what vehicles you can fly from it.

basic life-support loop

Closed-loop atmospheric control — recycles CO₂ to O₂ and manages humidity.

A basic environmental control and life support sub-system providing atmospheric revitalisation: CO₂ removal, O₂ generation via water electrolysis, trace contaminant control, and humidity management. Designed for a small crew in a pressurised module.

Real-world use · The International Space Station uses the Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS), which includes the Carbon Dioxide Removal Assembly (CDRA), the Oxygen Generation Assembly (OGA) using electrolysis, and the Water Recovery System (WRS). These systems recycle ~90% of water from humidity, urine, and other sources. Without them, resupply would be prohibitively expensive.

  • When · 1960s (basic Gemini systems) through present (ISS ECLSS).
  • Where · Any crewed spacecraft or habitat. Scaling up to closed ecological systems (biospheres) is an active research area.

Why it matters · Life support forces you to think in closed loops rather than linear flows. On Earth, you exhale CO₂ and it is absorbed by plants. On a space station, you must actively remove it or you die within hours. The same logic applies to water, waste, and atmosphere composition. The closed-loop life support system is the physical implementation of circular economy thinking: waste output of one process is input to another. CO₂ → electrolysis → O₂; condensed water → filtration → drinking water. In Conduvia, this module enables sustained lunar or orbital base operations.

demo ice ISRU extractor

In-situ resource utilisation demo unit — extracts water ice from lunar regolith.

A demonstration-scale ISRU (In-Situ Resource Utilisation) system designed to excavate and thermally process permanently-shadowed lunar regolith to extract water ice, then electrolyse it into hydrogen and oxygen for propellant or life support.

Real-world use · NASA's MOXIE experiment on Perseverance demonstrated oxygen production from Martian CO₂. Lunar ISRU for water extraction targets permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) at the poles where ice deposits have been confirmed by orbital spectroscopy and the LCROSS impact. Producing propellant in-situ is the key to economically viable lunar surface operations — launching all propellant from Earth is extremely expensive.

  • When · 2020s (demonstration missions); operational systems projected for 2030s.
  • Where · Lunar south pole permanently shadowed craters (Shackleton, Haworth, Nobile) where water ice concentrations are highest.

Why it matters · ISRU is the concept that breaks the fundamental limitation of space exploration: you cannot carry everything you need from Earth. If you can extract water from lunar ice, you have propellant (H₂/O₂) for rockets, water for life support, and oxygen for breathing — all from local resources. This is the T6 version of the same idea introduced in T0 by foraging: use what's already where you are rather than carrying everything. The difference is scale and technology. In Conduvia, the ISRU extractor is a prerequisite for self-sustaining off-world operations.

distilled LOX propellant

Liquid oxygen (LOX) — the oxidizer half of kerolox and hydrolox rocket engines.

Cryogenic liquid oxygen (-183 °C) produced by fractional distillation of air and used as the oxidizer in liquid-propellant rocket engines. Provides the oxygen for combustion without carrying an air supply; LOX has a much higher density than gaseous oxygen and allows compact propellant tanks.

Real-world use · Liquid oxygen as rocket oxidizer was proposed by Robert Goddard and Konstantin Tsiolkovsky independently. The first LOX/gasoline rocket flight was Goddard's 1926 launch. LOX is produced in bulk by the Linde-Frankl process — air is compressed, cooled, and fractionated. It is pale blue, highly reactive, and must be handled with care to avoid contact with organic materials.

  • When · 1926 (first flight) onward; industrial LOX since the 1890s.
  • Where · Air separation units co-located with launch facilities to minimise cryogen boil-off during transport.

Why it matters · LOX is the oxidizer that makes chemical rocketry possible — in space, there is no atmospheric oxygen, so rockets must carry their own. The cryogenic nature of LOX (-183 °C) imposes major engineering constraints: insulated tanks, cryogenic-rated seals, controlled venting to prevent overpressure, and rapid topping-off before launch as boil-off removes propellant continuously. In Conduvia, the LOX production chain (air separation → distillation → cryogenic storage) represents industrial gas processing at scale.

enriched uranium fuel rod

Slightly enriched UO₂ ceramic pellets in zircaloy cladding — the reactor fuel element.

A fuel assembly containing uranium dioxide pellets enriched to 3–5% U-235 (natural uranium is 0.7%) pressed into ceramic form and clad in zirconium alloy tubes. The ceramic form is chosen for stability at extreme temperatures; zircaloy cladding provides a structural and containment barrier while being nearly transparent to neutrons.

Real-world use · Uranium enrichment is the most technically demanding step in the nuclear fuel cycle. Natural uranium must be converted to UF₆ gas, then processed through gaseous diffusion or centrifuge cascades to increase the U-235 fraction. The fuel fabrication step then converts enriched uranium back to ceramic UO₂, pressed into pellets, sintered, and clad in tubes.

  • When · 1940s (enrichment development for weapons); commercial fuel fabrication 1950s onward.
  • Where · Enrichment facilities (centrifuge cascades); fuel fabrication plants; delivered to reactor sites under strict safeguards.

Why it matters · The fuel rod embodies the nuclear fuel cycle — one of the most complex industrial supply chains humans operate. Mine → mill → convert → enrich → fabricate → operate → cool → reprocess or store. Each step requires specialised infrastructure and strict material accounting. The ceramic fuel form is a deliberate engineering choice: UO₂ melts at 2865 °C, far above operating temperatures, and if cladding fails the ceramic holds fission products rather than releasing them. In Conduvia, fuel rods are the input to the nuclear reactor and represent the peak of the T6 material processing chain.

kerolox test rocket engine

RP-1/LOX first-stage engine — the workhorse of early orbital access.

A regeneratively-cooled liquid-propellant rocket engine burning refined kerosene (RP-1) with liquid oxygen (LOX). The kerolox combination offers high density and good specific impulse for first-stage use, with decades of flight heritage. This unit is a development engine validated on the test stand before flight.

Real-world use · Kerolox engines power some of the most prolific launchers in history: the R-7 family (Soyuz), the Falcon 9/Falcon Heavy, and the Saturn V first stage (F-1). The kerosene/LOX combination was chosen over hydrogen because RP-1 has a higher energy density by volume, is easier to store, and turbopumps handle it more reliably than cryogenic hydrogen at the engineering maturity of the 1960s.

  • When · 1950s onward; the R-7 flew in 1957, Falcon 9 first flew 2010.
  • Where · Engine test facilities first; then launch pads once qualification is complete.

Why it matters · Rocket engines are the single most thermodynamically demanding machine humanity builds routinely. Chamber pressures of 200 bar, combustion temperatures of 3500 K, and structural mass fractions of 1–2% of thrust force — the engineering margins are extremely tight. Regenerative cooling (routing propellant through channels in the nozzle wall before it enters the chamber) is what makes the structure survive combustion temperatures that would melt any known material. In Conduvia, this engine is the proof-of-concept for the orbital stack. You test it on the stand, validate performance data, and then integrate it into the launch vehicle.

light-water nuclear reactor

Pressurised or boiling water fission reactor — high power density, no combustion.

A thermal fission reactor using slightly enriched uranium fuel, ordinary water (H₂O) as both moderator and coolant, and a reactor pressure vessel to contain the primary circuit. Produces steam to drive turbines for electricity generation at power densities no chemical fuel can approach.

Real-world use · Light-water reactors (PWR and BWR) produce roughly 70% of all nuclear electricity worldwide. The design emerged from the US Navy's submarine propulsion programme in the 1950s under Admiral Rickover. The pressurised water concept was chosen for its inherent negative temperature coefficient of reactivity — as the core heats up, the reaction rate naturally decreases, providing passive safety.

  • When · First submarine (USS Nautilus) 1955; first commercial PWR (Shippingport) 1958.
  • Where · Coastal or riverine locations for cooling water supply; remote from population centres for safety radius.

Why it matters · The light-water reactor is the step where energy production breaks free of combustion entirely. Every previous tier burns something: wood, charcoal, coke, coal gas, oil. The reactor fissions uranium — a physical process that releases orders of magnitude more energy per kilogram than any chemical reaction. The challenge is not producing the energy but controlling it and converting it to usable forms (electricity). The containment vessel, control rods, and emergency core cooling systems are all answers to the same question: how do you safely handle a process that runs at millions of degrees Celsius inside the fuel pellets?

lunar solar power plant

Large-area photovoltaic array for sustained lunar surface power — no atmosphere to scatter light.

A deployed photovoltaic array designed for the lunar surface. Without an atmosphere, solar irradiance is the full 1361 W/m² at all times the sun is visible. Combined with high-efficiency multi-junction cells, a lunar solar plant produces more power per square metre than an equivalent terrestrial array.

Real-world use · Solar panels on the ISS generate about 90 kW from 2500 m² of arrays. On the lunar surface, Artemis base camp planning calls for kilopower nuclear reactors for the polar base (where the sun is never high) and solar arrays for equatorial surface ops. SpaceX Starship's lunar variant and the ESA lunar surface power concepts both use solar as the primary power source where applicable.

  • When · ISS arrays operational 2000; lunar surface solar concepts in active development 2020s.
  • Where · Equatorial and mid-latitude lunar sites with continuous sun access. Polar sites need nuclear because of permanent shadow periods.

Why it matters · Lunar solar is more powerful per area than Earth solar because there is no atmosphere to scatter or absorb light. But it has a critical vulnerability: the lunar night lasts 14 Earth days. Any base that relies on solar alone needs either enormous battery storage or secondary power for the night cycle. This is the same intermittency problem as terrestrial renewables, scaled to 336-hour night cycles. In Conduvia, combining lunar solar with nuclear provides the redundant power that sustained operations require.

orbital three-stage rocket stack

Three-stage orbital launch vehicle — the result of the full Tier 6 build chain.

A complete orbital launch vehicle assembled from a first stage, second stage, and payload fairing. Three-stage architecture allows each stage to shed mass as propellant is consumed, enabling payloads to reach orbital velocity that a single-stage vehicle cannot achieve with chemical propellants.

Real-world use · Multi-stage rocketry was proposed by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in the 1890s and enabled by the Rocket Equation. Staging is necessary because no practical propellant gives enough specific impulse for a single-stage vehicle to reach orbit with a useful payload fraction. The Saturn V (3-stage), Soyuz (2-stage with strap-ons), and Falcon 9 (2-stage) all use staging for this reason.

  • When · 1940s (V-2 precursors) through present.
  • Where · Launch complexes with vertical assembly facilities. The stack is assembled vertically, transported to the pad, and fuelled for launch.

Why it matters · The three-stage rocket is the culmination of every tier in Conduvia. Its mass breakdown illustrates the challenge: at liftoff, propellant is ~90% of the vehicle's mass. The payload may be 2–3%. Everything in between — structure, engines, avionics, plumbing — must be as light as possible. The rocket equation (Tsiolkovsky's) states this precisely: delta-v = Isp × g₀ × ln(m_wet / m_dry). Higher specific impulse, or higher mass ratio, equals more delta-v — the only thing that matters for changing orbits.

refined kerosene propellant

Highly refined kerosene (RP-1) for rocket engine use — low-sulfur, narrow cut.

A highly refined grade of kerosene with tightly controlled chemical composition, extremely low sulfur and olefin content, and a narrow distillation range. Standard fuel for kerolox rocket engines; chosen for its volumetric energy density, stability, and compatibility with metal turbopump hardware.

Real-world use · RP-1 (Rocket Propellant-1) was developed in the 1950s as a standardised rocket fuel meeting MIL-P-25576 specification. It is refined from crude oil through fractional distillation, hydrotreatment, and strict quality control. Standard kerosene cannot substitute — contaminants cause coking in the regenerative cooling channels.

  • When · 1957 onward (Sputnik R-7 used RP-1 precursor); RP-1 specification formalised by 1959.
  • Where · Produced at petroleum refineries with specialised processing units; stored cryogenically if sub-cooled.

Why it matters · RP-1 illustrates that 'fuel' is not a single material — specification matters. The difference between road diesel and RP-1 is a long list of impurity limits and a controlled distillation cut. That specificity is what makes it work in a turbopump at 100 000 RPM without fouling the lines. In Conduvia, the refining chain from raw petroleum to RP-1 represents T6 chemical processing.

robotic regolith drill

Autonomous drill head for lunar or planetary surface excavation.

A remotely-operated or autonomous rotary-percussive drill designed to excavate compacted regolith or rock and feed it to an ISRU hopper. Hardened for abrasive regolith conditions and radiatively cooled for use in vacuum.

Real-world use · Regolith is highly abrasive due to the lack of weathering — particles are sharp and angular. Drill bits used in vacuum must be hardened beyond terrestrial standards. The ESA/NASA PILOT project and several commercial ventures are developing regolith excavation systems for near-term lunar ISRU missions.

  • When · 2020s development; operational systems projected for 2030s lunar surface.
  • Where · Lunar surface, particularly in permanently shadowed regions for ice access.

Why it matters · The regolith drill is mining technology adapted to an environment without water, atmosphere, or heavy machinery infrastructure. Compare it to T0's hammerstone: both are percussion-based excavation tools. The principles are identical; the engineering constraints are completely different. In space, every design choice must account for vacuum, extreme thermal cycling (-170 °C to +120 °C on the lunar surface), abrasive unweathered particles, and the impossibility of easy maintenance.

standard docking port

Hard-dock interface for joining spacecraft and station modules.

A mechanical and electrical interface assembly allowing two spacecraft to attach firmly, share power and data, and transfer crew and cargo between sealed volumes. Uses capture latches, alignment guides, and sealing gaskets for vacuum-tight connection.

Real-world use · The first docking in space occurred with Gemini 8 (1966). The International Docking System Standard (IDSS) was developed to allow spacecraft from different nations to dock to a common interface — the ISS uses both Russian APAS docking systems and the US NDS (NASA Docking System). SpaceX Dragon, Boeing Starliner, and future commercial vehicles all use a standard docking interface.

  • When · 1966 (first docking) onward; IDSS standardised 2011.
  • Where · On all spacecraft and station modules designed for rendezvous-and-docking operations.

Why it matters · The docking port is an interface standard — its entire value comes from standardisation. A non-standard docking port is useless; a standard one connects any conforming spacecraft to any conforming station. Interface standards are how complex systems scale. In Conduvia, standard ports enable modular station assembly — just as Conduvia's crafting uses standardised item IDs to connect recipes across tiers without hardcoding every combination.

vertical engine test stand

Vertical hot-fire stand — validate engine performance before flight integration.

A structural test facility that holds a rocket engine in the firing position, with propellant feed, ignition, and data-acquisition systems. Used to measure thrust, specific impulse, and combustion stability before the engine is qualified for flight.

Real-world use · Every rocket engine is test-fired extensively before flight. NASA Stennis Space Center and SpaceX's test facilities in Texas have fired engines for hundreds of thousands of cumulative seconds before any given design reaches a launch vehicle. Testing catches manufacturing defects, design anomalies, and material fatigue before they cause mission loss.

  • When · 1940s onward as a standard practice.
  • Where · Remote sites with propellant infrastructure and acceptable blast radius. Water is often piped in for cooling and acoustic suppression.

Why it matters · The test stand embodies the principle of progressive validation: test the component, then the sub-system, then the system, then the vehicle. This 'test before fly' approach is what separates modern engineered systems from early trial-and-error. In Conduvia it gates engine integration: you can't put an unvalidated engine into the orbital stack.

Every recipe in Conduvia — 1530 in total — pulled straight from the game’s recipe database. Each card shows what goes in, what comes out, where you make it, and how long it takes. Byproducts (a second or third output) are flagged, because real processing usually throws something useful — or annoying — off to the side.

Sulfur leaves as hydrogen sulfide, which the existing Claus chain can recover into useful sulfur. petroleum_hydrotreat_kerosene Lithium Acid Roast Kiln 2 crude lithium sulfate×2 tailings×1 beta-spodumene×2 sulfuric acid×1 → crude lithium sulfate×2 tailings×1 Lithium Acid Roast Kiln 200s T4 840 kJ +1 byproduct Bake beta-spodumene with concentrated sulfuric acid at ~250 C: lithium ion-exchanges onto the sulfate, leaving the alumino-silicate skeleton as inert residue. li_acid_bake mixed rare-earth sulfate×2 thorium residue (radioactive)×1 rare earth concentrate×2 sulfuric acid×2 → mixed rare-earth sulfate×2 thorium residue (radioactive)×1 Lithium Acid Roast Kiln 220s T5 925 kJ +1 byproduct Crack the concentrate by baking with sulfuric acid: the lanthanides go to soluble sulfates while the radioactive thorium drops out as a captured residue — the dirty secret of every rare-earth mine. ree_acid_bake Magnesium Electrolysis Cell 1 neodymium metal×2 oxygen gas×1 neodymium oxide×2 → neodymium metal×2 oxygen gas×1 Magnesium Electrolysis Cell 240s T6 460 kJ +1 byproduct Electrowin neodymium from a molten fluoride/oxide bath — enormously energy-hungry, which is most of why rare-earth metals are expensive. ree_reduce_neodymium Membrane Electrolysis Cell 1 chlorine gas×1 dilute cell caustic×2 hydrogen gas×1 purified brine×2 → chlorine gas×1 dilute cell caustic×2 hydrogen gas×1 Membrane Electrolysis Cell 120s T3 350 kJ +2 byproducts Electrolyse the purified brine across an ion-selective membrane: chlorine bubbles off the anode, hydrogen off the cathode, and sodium ions cross the membrane to leave caustic soda behind. 2 NaCl + 2 H2O -> Cl2 + H2 + 2 NaOH. The single biggest electricity draw outside the aluminium pots. ca_membrane_cell Powder Press and Sinter Furnace 3 sintered NdFeB magnet×2 slag×1 neodymium metal×2 iron ingot×1 boric oxide (B2O3)×1 → sintered NdFeB magnet×2 slag×1 Powder Press and Sinter Furnace 220s T6 240 kJ +1 byproduct Strip-cast and liquid-phase sinter neodymium, iron and boron into the Nd2Fe14B phase, then magnetise: a sintered NdFeB magnet, the strongest there is. Boron is small but non-negotiable — it is what makes the phase exist. nd_make_ndfeb_magnet tantalum capacitor×2 capacitor-grade tantalum powder×3 → tantalum capacitor×2 Powder Press and Sinter Furnace 80s T6 90 kJ Press and vacuum-sinter tantalum powder into a porous anode pellet, anodise an oxide dielectric onto it, and finish into a capacitor — the most compact, reliable capacitor in electronics, and the reason anyone bothers separating tantalum from niobium. ta_make_capacitor cemented carbide insert×4 tungsten carbide powder×4 cobalt cathode×1 → cemented carbide insert×4 Powder Press and Sinter Furnace 150s T5 300 kJ Liquid-phase sinter tungsten-carbide powder with a COBALT binder (~6-10%) into a cemented-carbide insert: WC-Co, the genuine hardmetal grade used in real cutting tools. Cobalt wets and bonds WC grains far better than the old nickel stand-in. w_cemented_carbide Precipitation Tank 8 phosphoric acid×2 raw gypsum ore×3 phosphate rock×3 sulfuric acid×3 → phosphoric acid×2 raw gypsum ore×3 Precipitation Tank 80s T5 +1 byproduct Treat phosphate rock with sulfuric acid to make phosphoric acid, dropping gypsum as a byproduct (wet process). The gypsum here is the phosphogypsum the real process leaves behind. phosphoric_acid_wet_process bisphenol-A×1 raw water×1 phenol×2 acetone×1 → bisphenol-A×1 raw water×1 Precipitation Tank 80s T5 +1 byproduct Condense two phenols onto one acetone over an acid catalyst, splitting out water, to build bisphenol-A. bpa_condense epichlorohydrin×1 salt lick×1 raw water×1 dichlorohydrin×1 sodium hydroxide×1 → epichlorohydrin×1 salt lick×1 raw water×1 Precipitation Tank 70s T5 +2 byproducts Caustic soda strips HCl from dichlorohydrin and snaps the epoxide ring shut, giving epichlorohydrin; the lost chlorine leaves as common salt. epichlorohydrin_dehydrochlorinate ammonium nitrate×1 nitric acid×1 ammonia gas×1 → ammonium nitrate×1 Precipitation Tank 40s T5 Neutralize nitric acid with ammonia to crystallize ammonium nitrate, a heavy nitrogen fertilizer. ammonium_nitrate_neutralize diammonium phosphate×1 phosphoric acid×1 ammonia gas×2 → diammonium phosphate×1 Precipitation Tank 55s T5 React phosphoric acid with ammonia to granulate diammonium phosphate, carrying both nitrogen and phosphorus. dap_ammoniate single superphosphate×2 phosphate rock×2 sulfuric acid×1 → single superphosphate×2 Precipitation Tank 60s T5 Acidulate phosphate rock with sulfuric acid to make the phosphorus plant-available (single superphosphate). superphosphate_acidulate aluminum hydroxide (gibbsite)×2 sodium hydroxide×1 sodium aluminate liquor×3 → aluminum hydroxide (gibbsite)×2 sodium hydroxide×1 Precipitation Tank 180s T3 35 kJ +1 byproduct Cool the supersaturated liquor and seed it with fine gibbsite. Over hours, Al(OH)3 crystallises out: NaAlO2 + 2 H2O -> Al(OH)3 + NaOH. The freed caustic soda is pumped back to digestion — the Bayer circuit recycles its own lye. al_precipitate_gibbsite PVC resin×2 vinyl chloride monomer×4 → PVC resin×2 Precipitation Tank 80s T5 Link vinyl chloride units into PVC resin (suspension polymerization). pvc_polymerize Reagent Filling Line 4 glass cell (water)×1 glass cell×1 raw water×1 → glass cell (water)×1 Reagent Filling Line 20s T3 15 kJ Charge a borosilicate cell with raw water and seal — a clear, inert canister. cell_fill_glass_water metal cell (sulfuric acid)×1 metal cell×1 sulfuric acid×1 → metal cell (sulfuric acid)×1 Reagent Filling Line 25s T4 20 kJ Charge a stainless cell with sulfuric acid. The stainless body earns its cost here — acid would eat an ordinary can. cell_fill_metal_acid metal cell (sodium hydroxide)×1 metal cell×1 sodium hydroxide×1 → metal cell (sodium hydroxide)×1 Reagent Filling Line 25s T4 20 kJ Charge a stainless cell with sodium hydroxide. Caustic in aluminium would dissolve the can and vent hydrogen; stainless holds it safely. cell_fill_metal_caustic metal cell (water)×1 metal cell×1 raw water×1 → metal cell (water)×1 Reagent Filling Line 20s T4 15 kJ Charge a stainless cell with raw water and seal it — the neutral reference fill. cell_fill_metal_water Refinery Tank Farm 6 hot asphalt paving mix×4 asphalt binder×2 crushed gravel×4 → hot asphalt paving mix×4 Refinery Tank Farm 80s T5 160 kJ Heat asphalt binder and coat crushed aggregate into hot-mix asphalt. This turns refinery bottoms into hardstand/road material instead of a sticky dead-end stockpile. audit_asphalt_gravel_to_paving_mix hot asphalt paving mix×4 asphalt binder×2 slag×4 → hot asphalt paving mix×4 Refinery Tank Farm 85s T5 170 kJ Use cooled metallurgical slag as angular aggregate in asphalt mix. Slag roads and pads are real, practical, and much better than letting slag pile beside the furnace forever. audit_asphalt_slag_to_paving_mix hot asphalt paving mix×1 asphalt binder×1 crushed gravel×1 → hot asphalt paving mix×1 Refinery Tank Farm Aggregate coated with asphalt binder. It is infrastructure, not decoration. audit_asphalt_service_pad asphalt service pad×1 hot asphalt paving mix×1 crushed gravel×1 → asphalt service pad×1 Refinery Tank Farm placeModel=asphalt_service_pad • Station: refinery_tank_farm itemdb_asphalt_service_pad_refinery_tank_farm refined diesel fuel×3 diesel/gasoil fraction×3 fine propellant filter×1 → refined diesel fuel×3 Refinery Tank Farm 70s T5 100 kJ Filter and finish the gasoil cut into a practical diesel fuel for dispatchable machinery. Not rocket-clean; very useful anyway. petroleum_finish_diesel Rotary Calciner Kiln 7 boric oxide (B2O3)×2 borax×2 → boric oxide (B2O3)×2 Rotary Calciner Kiln 90s T4 695 kJ Calcine borax dry to boric oxide — the boron the magnet phase needs. reb_calcine_boric_oxide alumina×2 aluminum hydroxide (gibbsite)×3 → alumina×2 Rotary Calciner Kiln 90s T3 695 kJ Fire the gibbsite white-hot in the rotary kiln to drive off its chemical water: 2 Al(OH)3 -> Al2O3 + 3 H2O. Out comes smelter-grade alumina, a free-flowing white sand. al_calcine_alumina niobium pentoxide (Nb2O5)×1 hydrofluoric acid×1 niobium fluoride raffinate×1 → niobium pentoxide (Nb2O5)×1 hydrofluoric acid×1 Rotary Calciner Kiln 90s T5 695 kJ +1 byproduct Hydrolyse and calcine the niobium fluoride to white Nb2O5, driving off (and recovering) HF for re-use in digestion. nb_calcine_oxide beta-spodumene×2 raw spodumene ore×2 → beta-spodumene×2 Rotary Calciner Kiln 180s T4 1385 kJ Decrepitate spodumene near 1100 C: the alpha crystal flips to the open beta form. Skip this and acid simply will not attack the ore — the step everyone forgets. li_decrepitate synthetic rutile×2 slag×1 raw ilmenite ore×2 coke fuel×1 → synthetic rutile×2 slag×1 Rotary Calciner Kiln 90s T3 695 kJ +1 byproduct Reductively roast ilmenite (FeTiO3) so the iron drops out as a metallic/oxide fraction, leaving high-grade synthetic rutile. Becher-style upgrading — clean the feed before chlorination so you are not burning chlorine on iron. ti_upgrade_ilmenite tantalum pentoxide (Ta2O5)×1 hydrofluoric acid×1 tantalum fluoride extract×1 → tantalum pentoxide (Ta2O5)×1 hydrofluoric acid×1 Rotary Calciner Kiln 90s T5 695 kJ +1 byproduct Calcine the separated tantalum fluoride to Ta2O5, again recovering HF. The purified oxide is the gateway to capacitor-grade metal. ta_calcine_oxide uranium dioxide (UO2)×3 raw water×2 yellowcake×1 hydrogen gas×2 → uranium dioxide (UO2)×3 raw water×2 Rotary Calciner Kiln 100s T6 770 kJ +1 byproduct Hydrogen-reduce yellowcake to uranium dioxide: U3O8 + 2 H2 -> 3 UO2 + 2 H2O. The first conversion step toward a fluoride. u_reduce_uo2 Sheet Metal Press 1 metal cell×2 stainless steel sheet×2 → metal cell×2 Sheet Metal Press 60s T4 90 kJ Deep-draw and seam-weld stainless sheet into an empty cell body. Stainless, not plain steel or aluminium, because this one container has to survive both acid and caustic fills. cell_form_metal Siemens CVD Reactor 1 electronic-grade polysilicon×1 hydrochloric acid gas×3 silicon tetrachloride×1 trichlorosilane×3 hydrogen gas×2 → electronic-grade polysilicon×1 hydrochloric acid gas×3 silicon tetrachloride×1 Siemens CVD Reactor 200s T4 380 kJ +2 byproducts The Siemens process: pass trichlorosilane and hydrogen over glowing silicon rods so hyper-pure silicon deposits atom by atom (SiHCl3 + H2 -> Si + 3 HCl). Recovers HCl for the chlorinator and sheds SiCl4 for redistribution. The single most energy-hungry step in all of electronics. si_siemens_polysilicon Solvent Extraction Mixer-Settler 2 neodymium oxide×1 cerium oxide×1 mixed REE raffinate×1 mixed rare-earth sulfate×2 → neodymium oxide×1 cerium oxide×1 mixed REE raffinate×1 Solvent Extraction Mixer-Settler 260s T5 150 kJ +2 byproducts The keystone: a long counter-current solvent-extraction cascade exploits vanishingly small solubility differences to peel the lanthanides apart — abundant cerium first, the prized neodymium next, the rest banked as raffinate. This single abstracted step stands in for hundreds of real mixer-settler stages. ree_sx_split niobium fluoride raffinate×1 tantalum fluoride extract×1 crude Nb/Ta fluoride liquor×2 → niobium fluoride raffinate×1 tantalum fluoride extract×1 Solvent Extraction Mixer-Settler 160s T5 130 kJ +1 byproduct The keystone separation: run the mixed liquor through an MIBK solvent-extraction column to split niobium from tantalum — chemical twins so alike that this is one of the hardest routine separations in metallurgy, and the reason tantalum is costly. nb_solvent_extract Steam Machine Shop 9 steam control valve×1 rolled steel plate×1 turned steel shaft×1 bronze ingot×1 → steam control valve×1 Steam Machine Shop Station: machine shop (steam) itemdb_control_valve_steam_machine_shop_steam basic gas cylinder×2 steel ingot×1 → basic gas cylinder×2 Steam Machine Shop 70s T3 90 kJ Deep-draw and spin a steel billet into a seamless high-pressure cylinder, empty and ready to fill. The reusable container behind every compressed-gas product. gas_fab_cylinder lamp filament DC supply×1 insulated copper wire×1 laminated armature core×1 wrought-iron magnet core×1 → lamp filament DC supply×1 Steam Machine Shop Station: machine shop (steam) itemdb_filament_supply_dc_machine_shop_steam polyethylene sheet×4 polyethylene resin×2 → polyethylene sheet×4 Steam Machine Shop 40s T5 Press polyethylene resin into flat sheet stock. pe_sheet_press polypropylene sheet×4 polypropylene resin×2 → polypropylene sheet×4 Steam Machine Shop 40s T5 Press polypropylene resin into flat sheet stock. pp_sheet_press PVC pipe×4 PVC resin×2 → PVC pipe×4 Steam Machine Shop 40s T5 Extrude PVC resin into rigid pipe. pvc_pipe_extrude fluid handler station×1 wrought-iron steam pipe×3 steam control valve×1 tank level sensor×1 rolled steel plate×2 → fluid handler station×1 Steam Machine Shop placeModel=station_fluid_handler • Station: machine shop (steam) itemdb_station_fluid_handler_machine_shop_steam vent stack×1 rolled steel plate×5 steel rivet×8 wrought-iron steam pipe×1 → vent stack×1 Steam Machine Shop placeModel=station_vent_stack • Station: machine shop (steam) itemdb_station_vent_stack_machine_shop_steam laboratory vacuum pump×1 rolled steel plate×1 wrought-iron steam pipe×1 insulated copper wire×1 leather flat belt×1 → laboratory vacuum pump×1 Steam Machine Shop placeModel=vacuum_pump_lab • Station: machine shop (steam) itemdb_vacuum_pump_lab_machine_shop_steam Steam Reformer 3 ethylene×1 propylene×1 methane gas×1 raw natural gas×3 → ethylene×1 propylene×1 methane gas×1 Steam Reformer 90s T5 630 kJ +2 byproducts Steam-crack the natural-gas liquids to light olefins — ethylene plus a share of propylene — leaving methane as the residual sales gas. Cracking is energy-heavy, so it requires live steam pressure from the pipe network. ethylene_steam_crack ethylene×2 propylene×1 methane gas×1 petroleum naphtha×3 raw water×1 → ethylene×2 propylene×1 methane gas×1 Steam Reformer 100s T5 700 kJ +2 byproducts Steam-crack naphtha into olefins. This is the more refinery-grounded cousin of natural-gas-liquids cracking and gives plastics a real oil-fed route. petroleum_naphtha_steam_crack hydrogen gas×4 carbon dioxide gas×1 synthesis gas×3 raw water×1 → hydrogen gas×4 carbon dioxide gas×1 Steam Reformer 70s T4 490 kJ +1 byproduct Water-gas shift: CO + H2O -> CO2 + H2. Convert the carbon monoxide in syngas into still more hydrogen, leaving CO2 to vent or capture. This is the cheap bulk-hydrogen route most ammonia and refining actually run on. smr_water_gas_shift Steam Rolling Mill 1 stainless steel sheet×1 stainless steel ingot×2 → stainless steel sheet×1 Steam Rolling Mill chemName=StainlessSteel,formula=FeNiCr • Station: rolling_mill_steam itemdb_stainless_steel_sheet_rolling_mill_steam Submerged Arc Furnace 1 metallurgical-grade silicon×1 carbon dioxide gas×2 raw silica ore×2 coke fuel×2 → metallurgical-grade silicon×1 carbon dioxide gas×2 Submerged Arc Furnace 120s T3 260 kJ +1 byproduct Reduce quartz with carbon in a submerged-arc furnace at ~1900C: SiO2 + 2 C -> Si + 2 CO. Brutally energy-hungry (~11 kWh/kg), and the product is still only ~98% silicon — metallurgical grade, good for alloys but far too dirty for chips. si_carbothermic_silicon Survival Campfire 1 raw water×1 ice block×1 → raw water×1 Survival Campfire 30s T0 8 kJ Melt ice into raw water. It still needs boiling/treatment before safe drinking. audit_melt_ice_to_water Trip Hammer 1 crushed bauxite×2 stone dust×1 raw bauxite ore×2 → crushed bauxite×2 stone dust×1 Trip Hammer 30s T2 16 kJ +1 byproduct Mill the bauxite fine so hot caustic can reach every grain. No flotation here — bauxite is refined chemically, not concentrated mechanically. al_crush_bauxite Uranium Conversion Reactor 2 enriched UO2 powder×1 hydrofluoric acid×2 enriched UF6 (LEU)×1 raw water×2 hydrogen gas×1 → enriched UO2 powder×1 hydrofluoric acid×2 Uranium Conversion Reactor 110s T7 160 kJ +1 byproduct Hydrolyse and hydrogen-reduce enriched UF6 back to UO2 powder, recovering the fluorine as HF (fed straight back to conversion). Closing the fluorine loop is what makes conversion economic. u_reconvert_uo2_powder uranium tetrafluoride (UF4)×1 raw water×2 uranium dioxide (UO2)×1 hydrofluoric acid×4 → uranium tetrafluoride (UF4)×1 raw water×2 Uranium Conversion Reactor 100s T6 140 kJ +1 byproduct React UO2 with hydrogen fluoride: UO2 + 4 HF -> UF4 + 2 H2O. As-cut wafers are matte and saw-damaged — ready for rugged devices or for polishing. si_slice_wafer Workbench 2 A-frame gin pole×1 rough timber beam×3 rope×4 sheave×1 iron strap×2 → A-frame gin pole×1 Workbench 75s T1 A guyed lifting mast — two legs lashed at the head, stayed with rope, a sheave at the top. Swing heavy timber and cut stone up onto a wall with it. laminate×2 beta-cloth cover×1 epoxy resin×1 copper foil×2 → copper-clad laminate×2 PCB Fabrication Line 70s T5 130 kJ Press glass cloth, epoxy resin and copper foil into FR-4-like copper-clad laminate. cf_press_copper_clad_laminate blank control PCB×2 solder-masked PCB panel×1 tin-lead solder×1 → blank control PCB×2 PCB Fabrication Line 45s T5 80 kJ Tin the pads and cut the panel into finished bare control boards. cf_finish_control_pcb drilled PCB panel×1 etched PCB panel×1 cemented carbide insert×1 → drilled PCB panel×1 PCB Fabrication Line 45s T5 90 kJ Drill component and mounting holes with carbide tooling. cf_drill_pcb etched PCB panel×1 photoresist PCB panel×1 logic photomask×1 ferric chloride etchant×1 → etched PCB panel×1 PCB Fabrication Line 65s T5 100 kJ Expose the trace pattern and etch away unprotected copper, leaving the circuit traces. cf_etch_pcb_traces photoresist PCB panel×1 copper-clad laminate×1 photoresist resin×1 → photoresist PCB panel×1 PCB Fabrication Line 40s T5 70 kJ Coat the copper panel with photoresist so the trace artwork can be imaged. cf_coat_pcb_photoresist solder-masked PCB panel×1 drilled PCB panel×1 epoxy resin×1 titanium dioxide×1 → solder-masked PCB panel×1 PCB Fabrication Line 55s T5 90 kJ Apply and cure insulating solder mask, leaving only the solder pads open. cf_apply_solder_mask Powder Press and Sinter Furnace 5 ceramic IC package×2 porcelain pin insulator×2 copper foil×1 → ceramic IC package×2 Powder Press and Sinter Furnace 70s T5 150 kJ Sinter small ceramic packages around copper leadframes so chip dies can be handled and soldered. cf_make_ceramic_ic_package agglomerated cork×1 cork oak bark×2 → agglomerated cork×1 Powder Press and Sinter Furnace 70s T6 90 kJ Granulate cork oak bark and bake it under pressure until its own resins bind it into board. re_cork_agglomerate uranium dioxide pellet×4 enriched UO2 powder×2 → uranium dioxide pellet×4 Powder Press and Sinter Furnace 120s T7 200 kJ Press the UO2 powder into pellets and sinter near 1700 C into dense, hard ceramic cylinders — the actual fuel, fingertip-sized and good for years in-core. u_press_sinter_pellet PTFE seal blank×2 PTFE resin×1 → PTFE seal blank×2 Powder Press and Sinter Furnace 80s T6 110 kJ Press and sinter PTFE resin into machinable seal blanks. space_press_ptfe_seal_blank sintered tungsten rod×1 tungsten metal powder×4 → sintered tungsten rod×1 Powder Press and Sinter Furnace 180s T5 360 kJ Press the powder into a bar and sinter it near 2500 C until the grains weld solid — making a dense tungsten rod without ever melting the metal. This is powder metallurgy: the only way to consolidate the unmeltable. w_press_sinter_rod Precipitation Tank 3 ammonium hexachloroiridate×1 iridium residue×1 chlorine gas×2 ammonium chloride×2 → ammonium hexachloroiridate×1 Precipitation Tank 130s T6 180 kJ Chlorinate the residue to soluble iridium chloride and precipitate it with ammonium chloride as ammonium hexachloroiridate. re_ammonium_hexachloroiridate epoxy resin×1 salt lick×2 raw water×1 bisphenol-A×1 epichlorohydrin×2 sodium hydroxide×2 → epoxy resin×1 salt lick×2 raw water×1 Precipitation Tank 110s T5 +2 byproducts Couple bisphenol-A with epichlorohydrin under caustic soda (the caustic-coupling process) to make liquid epoxy resin (DGEBA). The displaced chlorine leaves as salt. epoxy_resin_couple iridium residue×1 PGM concentrate×1 nitric acid×1 hydrochloric acid gas×3 → iridium residue×1 Precipitation Tank 120s T6 170 kJ Digest the concentrate in aqua regia (nitric + hydrochloric); Pt, Pd and Au dissolve, leaving an insoluble Ir/Rh/Ru residue. re_iridium_residue Reactor Assembly Bay 1 light-water nuclear reactor×1 enriched uranium fuel rod×4 hafnium control rod×2 rolled steel plate×6 steam control valve×2 laboratory vacuum pump×1 three-phase AC generator×1 → light-water nuclear reactor×1 Reactor Assembly Bay 400s T7 600 kJ Assemble fuel rods, hafnium control rods, a steel pressure vessel, steam valves, a vacuum/coolant pump and a three-phase generator into a light-water reactor: fission heats water, water drives the generator. The capstone of the nuclear branch. u_build_reactor Reagent Filling Line 2 refined kerosene propellant×4 hydrotreated kerosene×2 RP-1 quality sample×1 fine propellant filter×1 → refined kerosene propellant×4 Reagent Filling Line 110s T6 120 kJ Filter and certify hydrotreated kerosene into rocket-grade RP-1 propellant. The filter is required but abstracted as consumed so the line needs steady maintenance stock. space_make_rp1_propellant refined kerosene propellant×4 hydrotreated kerosene×2 RP-1 quality sample×1 fine propellant filter×1 → refined kerosene propellant×4 Reagent Filling Line Station: reagent_filling_line itemdb_propellant_kerosene_refined_reagent_filling_line Refinery Tank Farm 1 refined kerosene propellant×3 hydrotreated kerosene×3 fine propellant filter×1 RP-1 quality sample×1 → refined kerosene propellant×3 Refinery Tank Farm 90s T5 160 kJ Filter and certify hydrotreated kerosene as rocket propellant. The existing synthetic syngas route still works, but this is the grounded crude-oil route. petroleum_finish_rp1 Reverberatory Furnace 1 lithium cobalt oxide cathode×1 lithium carbonate (battery grade)×1 roasted cobalt oxide×2 → lithium cobalt oxide cathode×1 Reverberatory Furnace Station: reverberatory_furnace itemdb_cathode_lithium_cobalt_oxide_reverberatory_furnace Rotary Calciner Kiln 3 Shell-405 catalyst×1 alumina×1 iridium sponge×1 → Shell-405 catalyst×1 Rotary Calciner Kiln 90s T6 150 kJ Impregnate an alumina support with iridium sponge and calcine into a Shell-405 hydrazine-decomposition catalyst bed. re_catalyst_shell405 zero-expansion glass-ceramic×1 lithium-aluminosilicate melt×1 → zero-expansion glass-ceramic×1 Rotary Calciner Kiln 160s T6 180 kJ Hold the glass at its nucleation temperature so crystals grow through it, yielding a near-zero-expansion glass-ceramic. re_ceramize_zerodur tungsten trioxide×2 ammonia gas×1 raw water×1 ammonium paratungstate (APT)×2 → tungsten trioxide×2 ammonia gas×1 raw water×1 Rotary Calciner Kiln 90s T4 695 kJ +2 byproducts Calcine APT to canary-yellow tungsten trioxide: it decomposes to WO3 + NH3 + H2O, and the ammonia is captured and piped back to the crystalliser. Clean oxide out, reagent recovered. w_calcine_apt Sheet Metal Press 3 anti-slosh baffle×2 aluminum sheet×1 → anti-slosh baffle×2 Sheet Metal Press 40s T6 70 kJ Press aluminum ring baffles that damp propellant slosh inside the tank. re_baffle_antislosh burst disk rupture panel×2 stainless steel sheet×1 boiler pressure sensor×1 → burst disk rupture panel×2 Sheet Metal Press 50s T6 70 kJ Press and score calibrated rupture disks for one-use overpressure relief. space_make_burst_disk parabolic dish reflector×1 aluminum sheet×3 turned steel shaft×1 limit position sensor×1 → parabolic dish reflector×1 Sheet Metal Press 90s T6 100 kJ Press and mount a steerable parabolic dish reflector. space_build_parabolic_reflector Siemens CVD Reactor 3 high-reflector cavity mirror×1 super-polished mirror flat×1 tantalum pentoxide (Ta2O5)×1 synthetic fused silica×1 → high-reflector cavity mirror×1 Siemens CVD Reactor 110s T6 170 kJ Sputter alternating quarter-wave tantala and fused-silica layers onto a polished flat to make a >99.99% dielectric high reflector. re_mirror_hr synthetic fused silica×2 silicon tetrachloride×1 oxygen gas×1 → synthetic fused silica×2 Siemens CVD Reactor 90s T6 150 kJ Flame-hydrolyse silicon tetrachloride into a pure SiO2 soot and fuse it into clear synthetic fused silica. re_fused_silica doped PN silicon wafer×2 polished silicon wafer×2 phosphoric acid×1 boron trifluoride×1 → doped PN silicon wafer×2 Siemens CVD Reactor 120s T6 180 kJ Dope polished wafers into PN junction solar-cell wafers. Phosphoric chemistry supplies the phosphorus side and boron trifluoride supplies the boron side; together they set the electric field that separates light-made charge. space_do_pn_doping TiCl4 Distillation Column 2 fractionated kerosene cut×2 synthetic kerosene×3 → fractionated kerosene cut×2 TiCl4 Distillation Column 120s T6 180 kJ Fractionate synthetic kerosene into the narrow middle-distillate cut used as RP-1 feedstock. This is deliberately a distillation-column job, not a magic furnace recipe. space_fractionate_kerosene_cut titanium tetrachloride×2 tailings×1 crude titanium tetrachloride×2 → titanium tetrachloride×2 tailings×1 TiCl4 Distillation Column 80s T4 90 kJ +1 byproduct Fractionally distil the crude tickle to strip iron, vanadium and silicon chlorides. Purity here decides the grade of metal at the far end — aerospace titanium starts with a clean distillation. ti_distill_ticl4 Uranium Conversion Reactor 1 uranium hexafluoride×1 uranium tetrafluoride (UF4)×1 fluorine gas×1 → uranium hexafluoride×1 Uranium Conversion Reactor 90s T6 150 kJ Fluorinate the green salt with elemental fluorine: UF4 + F2 -> UF6. The product sublimes to a gas at gentle heat — the one uranium compound you can pump through a centrifuge. u_fluorinate_uf6 Vacuum Arc Remelt Furnace 2 titanium ingot×1 titanium sponge×3 → titanium ingot×1 Vacuum Arc Remelt Furnace 180s T4 1385 kJ Crush and compact the sponge into an electrode, then vacuum-arc-remelt it into a dense, homogeneous ingot — often twice for aerospace grades. The vacuum keeps reactive titanium away from the oxygen and nitrogen it loves. ti_var_ingot Inconel turbine rotor×1 Inconel superalloy ingot×2 → Inconel turbine rotor×1 Vacuum Arc Remelt Furnace 90s T6 220 kJ Cast and finish a bladed Inconel turbine wheel that survives the gas-generator exhaust. re_turbine_rotor Vertical Engine Test Stand 2 flight-qualified kerolox engine×1 engine acceptance data pack×1 kerolox test rocket engine×1 distilled LOX propellant×12 refined kerosene propellant×6 nitrogen purge cart×1 helium pressurant cart×1 high-pressure gauge×2 high-temperature thermocouple×2 → flight-qualified kerolox engine×1 engine acceptance data pack×1 Vertical Engine Test Stand 240s T6 120 kJ +1 byproduct Static-fire the test engine on the stand. If the thrust, pressure, temperature and flow data are in family, the result is a flight-qualified engine plus its acceptance data pack. space_accept_kerolox_engine flight-qualified kerolox engine×1 engine acceptance data pack×1 kerolox test rocket engine×1 distilled LOX propellant×12 refined kerosene propellant×6 nitrogen purge cart×1 helium pressurant cart×1 high-pressure gauge×2 high-temperature thermocouple×2 → flight-qualified kerolox engine×1 engine acceptance data pack×1 Vertical Engine Test Stand +1 byproduct obtain=static_fire_acceptance • Station: test_stand_vertical itemdb_rocket_engine_kerolox_flight_test_stand_vertical Wafer Fab Line 9 diode junction wafer×1 polished silicon wafer×1 phosphoric acid×1 boron trifluoride×1 → diode junction wafer×1 Wafer Fab Line 75s T5 130 kJ Dope repeated PN junctions across a wafer for small signal diodes. cf_make_diode_junction_wafer diced logic die×8 passivated logic wafer×1 cemented carbide insert×1 → diced logic die×8 Wafer Fab Line 70s T5 130 kJ Saw the finished wafer into individual dies with hard carbide tooling. cf_dice_logic_die transistor junction wafer×1 polished silicon wafer×1 phosphoric acid×1 boron trifluoride×1 logic photomask×1 → transistor junction wafer×1 Wafer Fab Line 95s T5 170 kJ Pattern and dope nested NPN junctions across a wafer for discrete transistors. cf_make_transistor_junction_wafer doped transistor wafer×1 patterned logic wafer×1 phosphoric acid×1 boron trifluoride×1 → doped transistor wafer×1 Wafer Fab Line 110s T5 210 kJ Introduce phosphorus and boron dopants to form controlled n- and p-type transistor regions. cf_dope_transistor_regions patterned logic wafer×1 photoresist-coated wafer×1 logic photomask×1 hydrofluoric acid×1 → patterned logic wafer×1 Wafer Fab Line 95s T5 160 kJ Expose through the photomask, develop the resist, and etch openings through oxide. cf_expose_etch_logic_wafer metalized interconnect wafer×1 doped transistor wafer×1 copper foil×1 hydrogen gas×1 → metalized interconnect wafer×1 Wafer Fab Line 90s T5 180 kJ Deposit and pattern a metal interconnect layer so the transistors become a circuit. cf_metalize_interconnect oxidized silicon wafer×1 polished silicon wafer×1 oxygen gas×1 → oxidized silicon wafer×1 Wafer Fab Line 80s T5 170 kJ Thermally grow a controlled silicon-dioxide gate oxide on a polished wafer. cf_grow_gate_oxide passivated logic wafer×1 metalized interconnect wafer×1 synthetic fused silica×1 → passivated logic wafer×1 Wafer Fab Line 60s T5 120 kJ Seal the wafer under a protective silica passivation layer and open bond pads. cf_passivate_logic_wafer photoresist-coated wafer×1 oxidized silicon wafer×1 photoresist resin×1 → photoresist-coated wafer×1 Wafer Fab Line 50s T5 90 kJ Spin coat and soft-bake photoresist onto the oxidized wafer. cf_spin_photoresist_wafer Wire Drawing Bench 1 aluminum bond wire×8 aluminum ingot×1 → aluminum bond wire×8 Wire Drawing Bench 45s T5 70 kJ Draw very fine aluminum wire for die-to-package bonds. cf_draw_bond_wire Yellowcake Precipitator 1 yellowcake×1 tailings×1 uranium pregnant liquor×3 ammonia gas×1 → yellowcake×1 tailings×1 Yellowcake Precipitator 120s T6 110 kJ +1 byproduct Concentrate the liquor (solvent extraction / ion exchange) and precipitate ammonium diuranate with ammonia, then calcine it to bright-yellow U3O8 — yellowcake, the form uranium is actually shipped in. u_precipitate_yellowcake

docs.title: Tier 2 — Metal Ages: smelting & alloys
docs.text:
162 recipes

Absorption Tower 1 AOD Converter 1 Beehive Coke Oven 1 Blast Furnace 3 Camp Marker 5 Carving Bench 1 Caustic Digester Autoclave 1 Charcoal Clamp 1 Charcoal Drum Kiln 1 Charcoal Retort Kiln 1 Clay Bloomery 2 Clay Casting Pit 4 Clay Crucible 6 Copper Converter 2 Cupellation Hearth 1 Disc Pelletizer 2 DRI Shaft Furnace 1 Earthen Kiln 2 Electric Arc Furnace 4 Electric Ball Mill 6 Electric Induction Furnace 3 Electric Jaw Crusher 6 Electrolytic Refining Cell 1 Electrowinning Cell 5 Fire Refining Furnace 3 Flash Smelting Furnace 1 Forge Hearth 1 Froth Flotation Cell 9 Gathered from the world 13 Heap Leach Pad 3 Iron Anvil 4 Knapping Station 3 Lead Chamber 2 Magnesium Chloride Chlorinator 1 Magnesium Electrolysis Cell 1 Magnesium Flux Remelt Furnace 1 Magnetic Separator 2 Pidgeon Retort 1 Reagent Filling Line 1 Reverberatory Furnace 1 Roasting Pit 6 Rocker Box 2 Rotary Calciner Kiln 3 Sinter Strand 2 Sluice Box 2 Solvent Extraction Mixer-Settler 2 Steam Rolling Mill 5 Stone Anvil 4 Stone Mortar 3 Submerged Arc Furnace 3 Sulfur Burner 2 Tailings Re-Wash Box 1 Trip Hammer 12 Wet High-Intensity Magnetic Separator (WHIMS) 2 Workbench 4 Zinc Distillation Retort 1 Absorption Tower 1 sulfuric acid×3 oleum (fuming sulfuric acid)×2 raw water×1 → sulfuric acid×3 Absorption Tower 20s T4 12 kJ Bleed oleum down with a metered water add: H2S2O7 + H2O -> 2 H2SO4. Yields concentrated ~98% acid; part is drawn off as product, part recycled back to the absorption tower. acid_dilute_oleum AOD Converter 1 stainless steel ingot×2 slag×1 steel ingot×2 ferrochrome×1 ferronickel×1 burned lime (quicklime)×1 → stainless steel ingot×2 slag×1 AOD Converter 140s T4 390 kJ +1 byproduct Argon-oxygen decarburization: blow an O2/Ar mix through a chromium-bearing melt. Diluting the oxygen with argon lets carbon burn out while chromium does NOT oxidise away — so cheap high-carbon ferrochrome can be used. Makes ~75% of the worlds stainless steel. iron_aod_stainless Beehive Coke Oven 1 coke fuel×2 bituminous coal×3 → coke fuel×2 Beehive Coke Oven 600s T1 Coking bakes bituminous coal at 900-1100°C without oxygen, driving off sulfur, tar, and volatile compounds. The resulting coke burns at blast-furnace temperatures that charcoal cannot sustain. t1_coke_production Blast Furnace 3 crude lead bullion×2 slag×1 carbon dioxide gas×1 lead oxide sinter×2 coke fuel×1 limestone flux×1 → crude lead bullion×2 slag×1 carbon dioxide gas×1 Blast Furnace 220s T3 2155 kJ +2 byproducts Reduce the lead sinter with coke in a blast furnace to crude bullion. The silver in the ore reports almost entirely into the molten lead; iron and rock leave as slag. pb_blast_reduce pig iron ingot×2 slag×2 iron ore sinter×3 coke fuel×2 limestone flux×1 → pig iron ingot×2 slag×2 Blast Furnace 180s T2 1765 kJ +1 byproduct Charge sinter, coke and flux into the blast furnace. Coke burns to CO, which reduces the oxide (Fe2O3/Fe3O4 + CO -> Fe + CO2) as it descends; limestone fluxes the gangue to a fluid slag. Tap ~4%-carbon pig iron. A cleaner, more permeable burden than raw crushed ore. iron_blast_sinter pig iron ingot×1 crushed hematite×1 coke fuel×1 limestone nodule×1 → pig iron ingot×1 Blast Furnace Station: small blast furnace • Byproduct: slag_ironmaking itemdb_pig_iron_ingot_blast_furnace_small Camp Marker 5 stone anvil block×1 rounded river stone×4 medium dry log×1 rope×1 → stone anvil block×1 Camp Marker station=true,station_input=3,station_output=1 • Station: camp_marker_basic itemdb_anvil_stone_camp_marker_basic bronze axe×1 bronze axe head×1 wood haft×1 rope×1 → bronze axe×1 Camp Marker 240s T1 Fit the axe head into the hole in the handle and tie it tight; a cast (poured-metal) axe keeps its edge far longer than a chipped-stone one. e2_haft_bronze_axe bronze pickaxe×1 bronze pick head×1 wood haft×1 rope×1 → bronze pickaxe×1 Camp Marker 240s T1 Wedge the pick head onto the handle and bind it tight; lets you mine oxide and sulfide ores (the two main kinds of metal ore). e2_haft_bronze_pickaxe bronze shovel×1 bronze shovel blade×1 wood haft×1 rope×1 → bronze shovel×1 Camp Marker 240s T1 Pin or tie the blade to the handle; it moves far more soil per swing than the crude wooden shovel. e2_haft_bronze_shovel ore roasting pit×1 rounded river stone×6 loose dirt×4 medium dry log×2 → ore roasting pit×1 Camp Marker station=true,station_input=2,station_output=1,transport=chute • Station: camp_marker_basic itemdb_roasting_pit_camp_marker_basic Carving Bench 1 obsidian scalpel×1 pressure-flaked obsidian blade×1 construction wood×1 → obsidian scalpel×1 Carving Bench 90s T3 30 kJ Haft an obsidian micro-blade to a carved wooden handle: a surgical-grade scalpel whose edge cuts between cells for clean, low-scarring incisions. ob_make_scalpel Caustic Digester Autoclave 1 magnesium hydroxide×1 tailings×1 brine solution×2 burned lime (quicklime)×1 → magnesium hydroxide×1 tailings×1 Caustic Digester Autoclave 80s T3 60 kJ +1 byproduct Stir lime into magnesium-bearing brine; magnesium drops out as a milky Mg(OH)2 precipitate, the same trick used to win magnesium from seawater. mg_precipitate_hydroxide Charcoal Clamp 1 charcoal×3 medium dry log×10 → charcoal×3 Charcoal Clamp 600s T1 Earth-covered mound smoulders with restricted air. Most of the wood volatiles and much of its carbon burn off, so yield is poor and the burn needs many hours of tending. t1_charcoal_clamp Charcoal Drum Kiln 1 charcoal×7 medium dry log×10 → charcoal×7 Charcoal Drum Kiln 300s T2 A closed steel drum controls airflow far better than an open mound, so less of the charge is lost to combustion. Faster and roughly double the yield of the earth clamp. t2_charcoal_drum Charcoal Retort Kiln 1 charcoal×11 medium dry log×10 → charcoal×11 Charcoal Retort Kiln 180s T3 A sealed retort heats the wood from outside and admits no air, so almost none of the charge combusts. The wood-gas driven off is burned back under the retort to sustain heat. Highest yield and fastest of the three. t3_charcoal_retort Clay Bloomery 2 iron bloom×1 bloomery slag×4 crushed iron ore×5 charcoal×10 → iron bloom×1 bloomery slag×4 Clay Bloomery 360s T1 +1 byproduct Carbon monoxide from charcoal reduces FeO·OH to spongy metalite iron at ~1100-1200°C. The resulting bloom contains trapped slag and must be hammered to consolidate. t1_bloomery_bog_iron iron bloom×1 bloomery slag×4 roasted hematite×5 charcoal×10 → iron bloom×1 bloomery slag×4 Clay Bloomery 420s T1 +1 byproduct Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Hematite is harder and needs longer reduction time than bog iron, but produces a cleaner bloom with less sulfur. t1_bloomery_hematite Clay Casting Pit 4 bronze axe head×1 stone ingot mold×1 bronze ingot×2 charcoal×2 stone ingot mold×1 → bronze axe head×1 stone ingot mold×1 Clay Casting Pit 480s T1 +1 byproduct Melt the bronze over charcoal and pour it into the stone axe-head mold; knock it out once cool and grind the edge. e2_cast_bronze_axe_head bronze pick head×1 stone ingot mold×1 bronze ingot×3 charcoal×2 stone ingot mold×1 → bronze pick head×1 stone ingot mold×1 Clay Casting Pit 540s T1 +1 byproduct Pour the heavier two-pointed pick head; it uses more metal than an axe head, so it needs a longer, hotter melt. e2_cast_bronze_pick_head bronze shovel blade×1 stone ingot mold×1 bronze ingot×2 charcoal×2 stone ingot mold×1 → bronze shovel blade×1 stone ingot mold×1 Clay Casting Pit 480s T1 +1 byproduct Pour a wide, slightly curved blade; hammer the face smooth once cool so soil slides off instead of sticking. e2_cast_bronze_shovel_blade copper anode×2 blister copper×2 → copper anode×2 Clay Casting Pit 60s T2 45 kJ Cast blister/fire-refined copper into flat anodes for the electrorefining tankhouse. cu_cast_anode Clay Crucible 6 bronze ingot×9 copper ingot×9 tin ingot×1 → bronze ingot×9 Clay Crucible 150s T1 Controlled 9:1 Cu:Sn melt gives ~10% tin bronze — the historically documented sweet spot. Below ~6% Sn gives little hardness gain; above ~17% the alloy becomes brittle. t1_alloy_bronze bronze ingot×3 raw native copper×5 raw cassiterite ore×2 charcoal×8 → bronze ingot×3 Clay Crucible 240s T1 Smelting copper ore and cassiterite together without pre-measuring ingots produces an unpredictable tin fraction. Yield is lower than controlled alloying: 5 native copper + 2 cassiterite + 8 charcoal → 3 bronze here. The controlled route (same ore mass) smelts separately → 1 copper_ingot + 0.5 tin_ingot → alloy → 3 bronze AND you know the exact ~10% Sn. The Bronze Age switched to controlled alloying for consistency, not just yield. t1_cosmelt_crude_bronze copper ingot×1 stone ingot mold×1 raw native copper×5 charcoal×4 stone ingot mold×1 → copper ingot×1 stone ingot mold×1 Clay Crucible 120s T1 35 kJ +1 byproduct Native copper is melted in a clay crucible, then poured into a reusable stone ingot mold. The mold is required and returns after the pour. t1_smelt_native_copper copper ingot×1 stone ingot mold×1 raw native copper×5 charcoal×4 stone ingot mold×1 → copper ingot×1 stone ingot mold×1 Clay Crucible 180s T1 +1 byproduct Native copper is elemental metal — no chemical reduction needed. Heat to ~1085°C in a clay crucible, then pour into a reusable stone ingot mold. The mold is required and returns after the pour. t1_smelt_native_copper__1 tin ingot×1 raw cassiterite ore×4 charcoal×6 → tin ingot×1 Clay Crucible 210s T1 SnO₂ + 2C → Sn + 2CO₂. Carbon reduction at ~1100°C is required before the metallic tin can be tapped — its low melting point of 232°C only applies after reduction. t1_smelt_cassiterite tin ingot×2 tin concentrate (black tin)×2 charcoal×4 → tin ingot×2 Clay Crucible 150s T1 Smelt washed black tin (the gravity concentrate) instead of raw lump ore. With most of the gangue already washed away, the same crucible recovers far more metal per load — 2 concentrate -> 2 tin, against 4 raw ore -> 1 tin — and on less charcoal. This is why tinners always dressed the ore before the blowing-house. t1_smelt_cassiterite_concentrate Copper Converter 2 blister copper×1 sulfur dioxide gas×1 slag×1 copper matte×2 raw silica ore×1 → blister copper×1 sulfur dioxide gas×1 slag×1 Copper Converter 200s T2 560 kJ +2 byproducts Peirce-Smith two-blow. Slag blow: 2FeS + 3O2 -> 2FeO + 2SO2, then 2FeO + SiO2 -> fayalite slag. Copper blow: Cu2S + O2 -> 2Cu + SO2. Taps blister copper, ~98-99.5% Cu. cu_convert_blister nickel converter matte (Ni3S2)×1 slag×1 sulfur dioxide gas×1 nickel furnace matte×2 oxygen gas×1 → nickel converter matte (Ni3S2)×1 slag×1 sulfur dioxide gas×1 Copper Converter 100s T3 280 kJ +2 byproducts Blow air/oxygen through the molten matte in a Peirce-Smith converter to oxidise out the remaining iron (slagged with silica), leaving high-grade Ni3S2 converter matte and more SO2 for the acid plant. nis_converter Cupellation Hearth 1 silver dore×1 litharge (PbO)×1 silver-zinc crust×1 oxygen gas×1 → silver dore×1 litharge (PbO)×1 Cupellation Hearth 150s T3 630 kJ +1 byproduct Cupel the crust under an air blast: zinc and lead oxidise to litharge and are absorbed/skimmed, leaving a noble button of dore silver. The oldest assay there is. pb_cupellation Disc Pelletizer 2 indurated chromite pellet×3 crushed chromite ore×3 → indurated chromite pellet×3 Disc Pelletizer 45s T3 40 kJ Roll the chromite fines into green balls on the disc and fire them hard in the induration kiln. Indurated pellets keep the furnace burden permeable so reducing gas can climb through it. fcr_pelletize_chromite iron ore pellets×3 iron ore concentrate×3 raw clay×1 → iron ore pellets×3 Disc Pelletizer 80s T3 60 kJ Roll moist concentrate with ~1% bentonite binder (clay) into green balls on a disc, then indurate (fire) them hard. Uniform, high-Fe, high-strength pellets — the ideal direct-reduction feed. iron_pelletize DRI Shaft Furnace 1 sponge iron (DRI)×2 carbon dioxide gas×1 iron ore pellets×3 coke fuel×2 → sponge iron (DRI)×2 carbon dioxide gas×1 DRI Shaft Furnace 160s T3 1120 kJ +1 byproduct Solid-state reduction: pellets meet coal/CO in a shaft or rotary kiln below irons melting point. Oxygen leaves as CO2 while the metal never liquefies, yielding porous metallic sponge iron (DRI). The low-energy, scrap-substitute charge for electric-arc steel. iron_dri_coal Earthen Kiln 2 burned lime (quicklime)×1 limestone nodule×1 → burned lime (quicklime)×1 Earthen Kiln Station: earthen_kiln_updraft • Byproduct: CO2 itemdb_burned_lime_quicklime_earthen_kiln_updraft clay bloomery furnace×1 earthenware brick×8 raw clay×4 clay tuyere×2 charcoal×10 → clay bloomery furnace×1 Earthen Kiln transport=chute • Station: earthen kiln (updraft) itemdb_clay_bloomery_furnace_earthen_kiln_updraft Electric Arc Furnace 4 aerospace aluminum alloy×1 aluminum ingot×3 refined copper ingot×1 → aerospace aluminum alloy×1 Electric Arc Furnace chemName=Aerospace aluminum alloy • Station: arc_furnace_electric itemdb_alloy_aluminum_aerospace_arc_furnace_electric copper cathode×1 anode slime×1 blister copper anode×1 sulfuric acid×1 → copper cathode×1 anode slime×1 Electric Arc Furnace 120s T4 400 kJ +1 byproduct Hang the cast blister slab as an anode in a copper-sulfate and sulfuric-acid bath and pass direct current. Copper leaves the dirty anode and plates pure onto the cathode, while silver, gold, and selenium fall to the floor of the tank as anode slime. Slow and power-hungry, but it is the only way to reach the purity wire and electronics need. copper_electrorefine_cathode iron ingot×1 slag×1 sponge iron (DRI)×2 → iron ingot×1 slag×1 Electric Arc Furnace 70s T3 140 kJ +1 byproduct Melt sponge iron down to nearly pure, very-low-carbon iron ingots — electromagnet cores and clean alloying stock. This is why the mill replaced the anvil for sheet work. mill_copper_foil_machined copper plate×2 copper ingot×2 → copper plate×2 Steam Rolling Mill 60s T3 50 kJ Hot-roll copper ingot to plate stock. cu_form_plate copper rod×2 copper ingot×1 → copper rod×2 Steam Rolling Mill 45s T3 40 kJ Roll/forge ingot to round rod stock. cu_form_rod aluminum sheet×1 aluminum ingot×2 → aluminum sheet×1 Steam Rolling Mill chemName=Aluminum sheet,formula=Al • Station: rolling mill (steam) itemdb_metal_aluminum_sheet_rolling_mill_steam Stone Anvil 4 bronze shovel blade×1 bronze ingot×1 → bronze shovel blade×1 Stone Anvil 60s T1 Bronze is too hard to cold-hammer like copper, so it is melted and poured into a stone mould rested on the anvil. Once it sets, the cast blade is knocked out and the edges are trued up. The stone anvil doubles as the casting bench here. anvil_bronze_shovel_blade_cast copper foil×2 copper ingot×1 → copper foil×2 Stone Anvil 50s T1 Copper is soft enough to shape cold. Beat the ingot flat on the stone face, fold, and beat it down again until it spreads into thin sheet. The metal stiffens as you work it (it work-hardens), so smiths soften it in a fire between rounds (annealing). This cold-hammering on a stone anvil is the oldest metalworking there is. anvil_copper_foil_manual hammered copper nugget×1 raw native copper×3 → hammered copper nugget×1 Stone Anvil formula=Cu,chemName=Copper,elements=Cu:1 • Station: stone anvil itemdb_copper_nugget_hammered_anvil_stone copper rod×2 copper ingot×1 → copper rod×2 Stone Anvil 45s T1 Hammer the ingot out long and roll it round against the stone into rod stock for fasteners, contacts, and small parts. Anneal in the fire when it starts to stiffen so it does not crack. anvil_copper_rod_manual Stone Mortar 3 crushed iron ore×4 roasted bog iron×4 → crushed iron ore×4 Stone Mortar 60s T1 Era 3 (~30min hand work). Break roasted ore to walnut-fist size — too large makes cold spots, too fine chokes airflow. Reject white silica veins. Crushing dust scatters; no byproduct worth a slot. t1_crush_roasted_bog_iron raw cassiterite ore×1 stone dust×1 tin ore rock×2 → raw cassiterite ore×1 stone dust×1 Stone Mortar 55s T1 150 kJ +1 byproduct Crack and pan tin-stained stream rock for dense black cassiterite grains. Hand sorting works, but later stamping and washing recover much more. audit_sort_tin_ore_rock raw native copper×1 stone dust×1 copper ore rock×2 → raw native copper×1 stone dust×1 Stone Mortar 55s T1 150 kJ +1 byproduct Hammer copper-stained float rock apart and hand-sort visible native copper pieces from waste rock. This is low-yield hand beneficiation before mills and flotation exist. audit_sort_copper_ore_rock Submerged Arc Furnace 3 ferrochrome×2 slag×2 carbon dioxide gas×2 indurated chromite pellet×3 coke fuel×3 burned lime (quicklime)×1 → ferrochrome×2 slag×2 carbon dioxide gas×2 Submerged Arc Furnace 150s T4 380 kJ +2 byproducts Bury the electrodes in a charge of pellets, coke and lime and pour the power in: FeCr2O4 + 4 C -> Fe + 2 Cr + 4 CO. The carbon strips the oxygen, lime fluxes the Mg/Al/Si gangue into a fluid slag, and the CO off-gas burns off as CO2. Taps as high-carbon ferrochrome. One of the most energy-hungry steps in the whole tech tree. fcr_saf_smelt ferronickel×2 slag×2 reduced laterite calcine×3 coke fuel×2 burned lime (quicklime)×1 → ferronickel×2 slag×2 Submerged Arc Furnace 150s T4 360 kJ +1 byproduct Reduction-smelt the hot calcine in the electric (submerged-arc) furnace. Nickel and a controlled amount of iron drop out together as a dense crude ferronickel; the silicate gangue floats off as slag. ~99% of the nickel is recovered — the E and F of RKEF. fni_smelt_ferronickel ferrosilicon (FeSi)×1 carbon dioxide gas×1 raw silica ore×2 pig iron ingot×1 coke fuel×2 → ferrosilicon (FeSi)×1 carbon dioxide gas×1 Submerged Arc Furnace 130s T3 260 kJ +1 byproduct Smelt silica with iron and coke in a submerged-arc furnace to ferrosilicon — a steel deoxidiser, and here the reductant that will free magnesium from dolime. mg_make_ferrosilicon Sulfur Burner 2 sulfur dioxide gas×2 recovered sulfur×2 oxygen gas×2 → sulfur dioxide gas×2 Sulfur Burner 40s T4 85 kJ Burn recovered sulfur in air: S + O2 -> SO2. A cleaner SO2 feed for the contact sulfuric-acid plant than roasting pyrite — and, in the real world, the dominant modern route to acid. ng_burn_sulfur sulfur dioxide gas×6 roasted hematite×2 raw pyrite ore×4 → sulfur dioxide gas×6 roasted hematite×2 Sulfur Burner 50s T2 105 kJ +1 byproduct Dead-roast pyrite in excess air: 4 FeS2 + 11 O2 -> 2 Fe2O3 + 8 SO2. Drives off the SO2 acid feed AND leaves an iron-oxide cinder — the same roasted hematite the iron chain smelts. One of the oldest acid feedstocks; the other is captured copper-smelter SO2. acid_roast_pyrite Tailings Re-Wash Box 1 galena concentrate×1 tailings×8 → galena concentrate×1 Tailings Re-Wash Box 200s T1 Re-washing settled tailings scavenges the little galena the first pass missed. Low yield and slow, but nothing goes to waste. t1_tailings_retreat_galena Trip Hammer 12 chalcopyrite concentrate×2 raw chalcopyrite ore×3 → chalcopyrite concentrate×2 Trip Hammer formula=CuFeS2,chemName=Chalcopyrite,elements=Cu:1|Fe:1|S:2 • Station: stamp mill (manual trip hammer) itemdb_concentrate_chalcopyrite_stamp_mill_manual_trip_hammer copper dust×2 copper ingot×1 → copper dust×2 Trip Hammer 30s T1 File/grind ingot to copper powder for alloying and powder metallurgy. cu_form_dust crushed cassiterite×3 tailings×1 raw cassiterite ore×4 → crushed cassiterite×3 tailings×1 Trip Hammer 60s T1 +1 byproduct Stamp the lump cassiterite to a coarse sand so the dense tin oxide can be washed loose from the lighter rock. About a quarter is lost as fines to tailings, the same as the other stamp-mill feeds. t1_crush_cassiterite crushed chalcopyrite×5 stone dust×1 raw chalcopyrite ore×6 → crushed chalcopyrite×5 stone dust×1 Trip Hammer 45s T1 +1 byproduct Coarse stamp-crush to liberate chalcopyrite from gangue. ~1 in 6 reports to fines as stone dust. Muscle/trip-hammer — pay in time, not energy. cu_crush_chalcopyrite crushed chromite ore×2 stone dust×1 raw chromite ore×2 → crushed chromite ore×2 stone dust×1 Trip Hammer 30s T2 16 kJ +1 byproduct Crush friable lump chromite to an even grain. Chromite is brittle and sheds fines, so it is crushed deliberately and then re-agglomerated rather than charged as-mined. fcr_crush_chromite crushed oxide copper ore×2 stone dust×1 oxidized copper ore×2 → crushed oxide copper ore×2 stone dust×1 Trip Hammer 25s T1 12 kJ +1 byproduct Crush oxidized ore to a coarse, permeable gravel (12-50 mm). Oxide heaps want a COARSE crush — fine grinding would only choke acid percolation and burn extra acid on freshly exposed gangue. cu_crush_oxide crushed hematite×3 tailings×1 raw hematite ore×4 → crushed hematite×3 tailings×1 Trip Hammer 60s T1 +1 byproduct Stamp mill crushes lump hematite to a fine fraction suitable for blast furnace burden or wet separation. ~25% losses to tailings. t1_crush_hematite crushed magnetite×3 tailings×1 raw magnetite ore×4 → crushed magnetite×3 tailings×1 Trip Hammer 60s T1 +1 byproduct Crushed magnetite can be magnetically separated at higher tiers; for now it serves as a direct blast furnace feed. t1_crush_magnetite crushed slag×3 slag×4 → crushed slag×3 Trip Hammer 60s T2 Bloomery and furnace slag retains trapped iron particles. Crushing and re-feeding recovers a useful fraction — important when ore is scarce. t1_crush_slag ground chalcopyrite×4 stone dust×1 crushed chalcopyrite×5 → ground chalcopyrite×4 stone dust×1 Trip Hammer 60s T1 +1 byproduct Fine grind to ~75 micron flotation size. Over-grind sheds a little more stone dust. cu_grind_chalcopyrite limestone flux×2 burned lime (quicklime)×1 raw limestone ore×3 → limestone flux×2 burned lime (quicklime)×1 Trip Hammer 60s T1 +1 byproduct Crushed limestone (CaCO₃) is the flux for blast furnaces. Fines that pass through the screen partially calcine during crushing heat, yielding a quicklime byproduct (CaO). t1_crush_limestone_flux iron ore concentrate×1 iron ore rock×1 → iron ore concentrate×1 Trip Hammer Station: stamp_mill_manual_trip_hammer • Byproduct: tailings itemdb_ore_iron_concentrate_stamp_mill_manual_trip_hammer Wet High-Intensity Magnetic Separator (WHIMS) 2 iron ore concentrate×3 tailings×1 ground magnetite×4 → iron ore concentrate×3 tailings×1 Wet High-Intensity Magnetic Separator (WHIMS) 60s T4 55 kJ +1 byproduct Pull a high-grade iron concentrate from finely ground magnetite in a strong electromagnetic field. Grinding ahead of separation recovers far more iron than running crushed ore through the basic drum LIMS. (wet high-intensity magnetic separation) t4_whims_magnetite iron ore concentrate×3 tailings×1 ground hematite×4 → iron ore concentrate×3 tailings×1 Wet High-Intensity Magnetic Separator (WHIMS) 66s T4 60 kJ +1 byproduct Recover iron from finely ground hematite that the basic drum LIMS cannot catch — the high-intensity field grabs the weakly magnetic oxide, no coke reduction roast needed. (wet high-intensity magnetic separation) t4_whims_hematite Workbench 4 forge hearth×1 earthenware brick×6 raw clay×3 clay tuyere×1 bellows×1 → forge hearth×1 Workbench transport=chute • Station: workbench itemdb_forge_hearth_workbench iron anvil block×1 wrought iron bar×4 → iron anvil block×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_iron_anvil_block_workbench stone ingot mold×1 rounded river stone×4 → stone ingot mold×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_stone_mold_ingot_workbench iron hammer×1 iron hammer head×1 rope×1 fine forest twigs×2 → iron hammer×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_tool_iron_hammer_workbench Zinc Distillation Retort 1 zinc ingot×2 carbon dioxide gas×2 zinc oxide calcine×2 coke fuel×2 → zinc ingot×2 carbon dioxide gas×2 Zinc Distillation Retort 180s T3 1010 kJ +1 byproduct The old way: reduce the calcine with coke and distil the zinc off as vapour (zinc boils at 907 C), condensing it to metal. Energy-hungry but needs no electricity — the historic and Imperial-Smelting route. zn_retort_thermal

pig iron ingot×4 → steel ingot×3 slag×1 Bessemer Converter 300s T2 +1 byproduct The Bessemer blow forces cold air through liquid pig iron from tuyeres at the converter base. Oxygen in the air burns out carbon, silicon, and manganese in a violent 15-20 minute exothermic reaction — the heat released is so intense that no external fuel is needed after ignition. Carbon drops from ~4% to ~0.2-0.5%, producing steel. The blow must be stopped at the right carbon level; over-blowing produces wrought iron, under-blowing leaves cast iron. t2_bessemer_steel Blast Furnace 1 pig iron ingot×4 slag×3 crushed hematite×6 coke fuel×3 limestone flux×2 → pig iron ingot×4 slag×3 Blast Furnace 480s T2 +1 byproduct The blast furnace drives a continuous reduction column: coke burns to CO at tuyere level (~1600 degC), CO reduces Fe2O3 to iron as the burden descends, and limestone flux (CaO after calcination) reacts with gangue silica to form liquid slag (CaSiO3) that floats above liquid pig iron. Pig iron absorbs ~4% C from coke — it is hard but brittle. The slag must be tapped separately from the iron notch. t2_blast_furnace_pig_iron Camp Marker 1 leather flat belt×1 light tanned leather×1 brown dye×1 raw water×1 → leather flat belt×1 Camp Marker 70s T1 110 kJ Use tannin-rich brown dye while finishing leather belt stock. The straw stops cracking. Weaker than fired brick and unhappy in steady rain. bld_form_adobe adze×1 stone adze head×1 wood haft×1 rope×1 → adze×1 Camp Marker 240s T0 Seat the bit transverse on a knee-bend haft and lash it tight; the edge faces the worker. e1_assemble_adze basket (coiled)×1 curled bark strip×6 rawhide cord×2 → basket (coiled)×1 Camp Marker 35s T0 Coil long bark strips into a spiral and bind each turn to the last with cord. The result is a light carry-basket for forage, stone, and clay — it hauls loose material your hands cannot.
