It is lower yield than hide glue but historically useful. audit_hoof_keratin_to_glue grease (tallow)×1 raw animal fat×2 → grease (tallow)×1 Survival Campfire 240s T0 Melt the trimmed fat slowly over low heat, skim the clean fat (called tallow) off the crispy leftover bits, and let it cool until hard. e1_render_grease_tallow pitch×1 tar×2 → pitch×1 Survival Campfire 240s T0 Boil the tar down until the thin, watery parts cook off and it sets stiff — hard pitch that seals seams instead of staying sticky. e1_reduce_pitch Tailings Re-Wash Box 1 crushed gravel×4 tailings×6 crushed gravel×2 → crushed gravel×4 Tailings Re-Wash Box 90s T2 120 kJ Dewater and blend coarse tailings with crushed aggregate as low-grade engineered fill. It is not ore recovery; it is the realistic civil-engineering sink for inert sand and fines. audit_tailings_to_compacted_fill Trip Hammer 3 paper pulp×1 plant fibers×2 raw water×1 wood ash×1 → paper pulp×1 Trip Hammer 70s T1 180 kJ Soak plant fibre in water with a little wood-ash lye and beat it under the trip hammer into a pulp. ppr_pulp_fiber paper pulp×2 linen cloth×1 raw water×1 → paper pulp×2 Trip Hammer 60s T1 180 kJ Beat linen rag in water under the trip hammer into a fine, high-yield rag pulp. ppr_pulp_rag paper pulp×2 stripped log×1 raw water×1 slaked lime×1 → paper pulp×2 Trip Hammer 110s T1 200 kJ Cook wood with slaked lime and beat it into a coarse wood pulp at the trip hammer. ppr_pulp_wood Workbench 63 steel beam×1 rolled steel beam×1 steel rivet×4 → steel beam×1 Workbench 70s T4 Rivet up a steel span to carry heavy loads across wide openings no timber could manage. bld_build_beam_steel bellows×1 construction wood×1 raw animal hide×1 rope×1 → bellows×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_bellows_workbench block-and-tackle×1 sheave×3 rough board plank×2 rope×4 iron strap×2 → block-and-tackle×1 Workbench 60s T1 Two blocks of sheaves reeved with a single rope. Each fall of rope between the blocks divides the load again, so four falls let one person hold what four could not. The price is rope and travel: you haul four times the length to raise the load once. block_and_tackle_build_manual blank book×1 carbon ink×1 paper×2 plant thread×1 → blank book×1 Workbench 60s T1 90 kJ Use carbon ink to rule and mark a blank field notebook. Ink becomes part of the knowledge/questbook chain instead of stopping dead. audit_carbon_ink_write_book blank book×1 iron gall ink×1 paper×2 plant thread×1 → blank book×1 Workbench 60s T3 90 kJ Use permanent iron-gall ink for a durable lab notebook. This later ink is better for records and engineering notes. audit_iron_gall_write_book blank book×1 paper×5 light tanned leather×1 plant thread×2 animal glue×1 → blank book×1 Workbench 90s T1 70 kJ Fold and stitch paper sheets into a block, glue the spine, and bind it into leather covers to make a blank book. book_bind_blank capstan×1 rough timber beam×2 wooden shaft (round)×1 wooden power pole×2 iron strap×2 plain bearing (wood)×1 → capstan×1 Workbench 70s T1 A vertical drum turned by push-bars walked in a circle. Several people throw their weight against the bars at once, so a gang can drag loads — beached boats, raw timber, foundation stone — that no rope-pull ever could. Iron straps keep the drum from splitting under the strain. capstan_build_manual carving bench×1 rough board plank×3 rough timber beam×2 wooden peg×4 rope×1 → carving bench×1 Workbench placeModel=workbench • Station: workbench itemdb_carving_bench_workbench linen cloth×1 plant thread×3 → linen cloth×1 Workbench 120s T1 200 kJ Weave spun plant thread into a bolt of light, breathable linen-type cloth. tex_weave_linen_cloth wool cloth×1 wool yarn×3 → wool cloth×1 Workbench 120s T1 200 kJ Warp the loom and weave wool yarn into a bolt of warm, hard-wearing cloth. tex_weave_wool_cloth coarse screen×1 rough timber beam×2 rough board plank×2 wrought iron bar×2 → coarse screen×1 Workbench 55s T1 An iron-barred grizzly screen in a heavy timber frame. Tip crushed ore or gravel across it and the fines fall through while the oversize rolls off to be crushed again — the sorting step that keeps the later mills from choking on rock that is too big. coarse_screen_build_manual copperas×2 iron ingot×1 chamber acid (dilute H2SO4)×1 → copperas×2 Workbench 80s T3 110 kJ Dissolve iron in dilute sulfuric acid and evaporate to pale green copperas crystals (iron sulfate). ink_make_copperas counterweight×1 rough board plank×3 rounded river stone×12 rope×2 → counterweight×1 Workbench 45s T1 A stone-filled crate that lifts for you: let the weight fall and it raises the load on the other end of the rope. Deliberately heavy on stone — the whole point is the mass. Pair it with a gin pole or a treadle and gravity does the lifting. counterweight_build_manual wool felt×1 washed wool×2 raw water×1 → wool felt×1 Workbench 90s T1 200 kJ Agitate washed wool in hot water until the fibres lock together into a dense felt — no spinning needed. tex_felt_wool fire-starter bundle×1 tinder×1 deadwood×2 alder catkin cone×1 → fire-starter bundle×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_fire_starter_bundle_workbench concrete slab×1 wet concrete×4 steel rebar×2 → concrete slab×1 Workbench 120s T4 Cast a rebar slab to span wider and carry far more than timber. Heavy, so it needs solid supports beneath. bld_build_floor_concrete flywheel×1 construction wood×1 fieldstone×1 rope×1 → flywheel×1 Workbench placeModel=flywheel,station=true,transport=shaft • Station: workbench itemdb_flywheel_workbench concrete footing×1 cured concrete×4 steel rebar×1 → concrete footing×1 Workbench 90s T3 220 kJ Set cured concrete blocks and rebar into a heavy footing. Poured wet concrete is best, but cured blocks should still build foundations. audit_cured_concrete_to_foundation concrete footing×1 wet concrete×4 steel rebar×2 → concrete footing×1 Workbench 120s T4 Pour a rebar-tied concrete footing, the strongest anchor and the best base for tall or heavy builds. bld_build_foundation_concrete stone footing×1 cobblestone×6 lime mortar×2 → stone footing×1 Workbench 90s T2 Bed heavy stone in mortar to spread the load into the ground: a strong, low anchor for everything above. bld_build_foundation_stone geared gristmill×1 construction wood×8 fieldstone×4 wheel-and-axle×2 → geared gristmill×1 Workbench station=true,station_input=2,station_output=2 • Station: workbench itemdb_gristmill_geared_workbench holdfast×1 rough timber beam×1 wooden peg×3 rounded river stone×2 → holdfast×1 Workbench 35s T1 A wedge-and-peg arm that drops through a hole in the bench and pins your work flat with a tap, freeing both hands. Entirely wood and stone — no iron needed yet — but it is the difference between fighting a workpiece and working it. holdfast_build_manual carbon ink×2 black pigment×1 animal glue×1 raw water×1 → carbon ink×2 Workbench 45s T1 60 kJ Suspend black carbon pigment in glue and water to make a writing ink. ink_make_carbon iron gall ink×2 curled bark strip×2 copperas×1 raw water×1 → iron gall ink×2 Workbench 70s T1 70 kJ Steep bark tannin in water and react it with copperas to make dark, permanent iron-gall ink. ink_make_iron_gall lever press×1 construction wood×1 fieldstone×1 rope×1 → lever press×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_lever_press_workbench lime wash×1 burnt shell lime×2 raw water×1 → lime wash×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_lime_wash_workbench lye×1 wood ash×2 raw water×1 → lye×1 Workbench 50s T1 40 kJ Trickle water through wood ash to leach out a caustic lye solution. soap_leach_lye brick pier×1 fired clay brick×8 cement mortar×2 → brick pier×1 Workbench 90s T3 Lay fired brick in mortar into a stout pier: heavy, fireproof, and stiff against both load and sway. bld_build_pillar_brick concrete column×1 reinforced concrete×3 → concrete column×1 Workbench 90s T4 Cast a rebar-cored column, the workhorse vertical support for tall builds. bld_build_pillar_concrete post mill (windmill)×1 construction wood×10 rope×4 wheel-and-axle×2 tailpole (windmill yaw)×1 → post mill (windmill)×1 Workbench Optional late-T1 • Station: workbench itemdb_post_mill_windmill_workbench potter's wheel (kick)×1 rough timber beam×2 wooden shaft (round)×1 rounded river stone×6 plain bearing (wood)×1 wooden peg×4 → potter's wheel (kick)×1 Workbench 80s T1 A heavy stone disk keyed to a vertical shaft on a wooden bearing. You kick the flywheel to keep it spinning and shape the clay on the head up top — the momentum of the stone does the work your free hand cannot. Building it is the gate to throwing pots instead of coiling them. potters_wheel_kick_build_manual potter's wheel (kick)×1 construction wood×1 fieldstone×1 → potter's wheel (kick)×1 Workbench late-t0,quality-of-life • Station: workbench itemdb_potters_wheel_kick_workbench pulley×1 sheave×1 wooden dowel×1 iron strap×1 → pulley×1 Workbench 35s T1 A grooved sheave turning on a dowel pin in an iron-strapped block. On its own it just changes the direction of a rope — but that is enough to pull down on a load instead of lifting up on it, and it is the building block every heavier rig is made from. pulley_build_manual pulley×1 sheave×1 construction wood×1 rope×1 → pulley×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_pulley_workbench quern (rotary)×1 fieldstone×4 construction wood×2 → quern (rotary)×1 Workbench station=true,station_input=2,station_output=1 • Station: workbench itemdb_quern_rotary_workbench riffle insert (sluice)×1 construction wood×2 → riffle insert (sluice)×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_riffle_insert_sluice_workbench rocker box×1 construction wood×8 fieldstone×2 → rocker box×1 Workbench station=true,station_input=1,station_output=2 • Station: workbench • Byproduct: tailings itemdb_rocker_box_workbench tiled roof×1 rough timber beam×2 rough board plank×2 clay roof tile×10 → tiled roof×1 Workbench 100s T2 Lap fired clay tiles over a timber frame. Heavy and slower to build, but fireproof and long-lasting. bld_build_roof_tiled rope-walk jig×1 rough timber beam×3 wooden gear (peg-toothed)×2 iron strap×2 rope×1 → rope-walk jig×1 Workbench 70s T1 A long geared frame that twists many yarns into heavy rope in one pass, hook turning against hook down the length of the walk. It is the leap from hand-laid cordage to real line — the rope a capstan or a gin pole actually needs. rope_walk_jig_build_manual screw jack (wooden)×1 rough timber beam×1 wooden dowel×2 forged iron crank×1 iron strap×1 → screw jack (wooden)×1 Workbench 60s T1 A hand-cut hardwood screw running in a timber nut. It lifts slowly but holds its load without slipping and without anyone holding the crank — exactly what you want when truing up a beam or raising a sill a hair at a time. screw_jack_wooden_build_manual sheave×1 construction wood×1 fieldstone×1 → sheave×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_sheave_workbench sieve×1 rough board plank×2 plant fibers×6 rawhide cord×2 → sieve×1 Workbench 40s T1 A woven fiber mesh stretched in a wooden hoop. Shake flour, sand, or wet clay through it and it sorts the fine from the coarse — the first tool that grades material by size instead of by eye. Tempering clay through a sieve is what stops fired pots from cracking. sieve_build_manual sluice box×1 construction wood×10 fieldstone×4 riffle insert (sluice)×1 → sluice box×1 Workbench station=true,station_input=1,station_output=2 • Station: workbench • Byproduct: tailings itemdb_sluice_box_workbench sluice trough×1 rough board plank×5 wooden peg×4 rope×2 → sluice trough×1 Workbench 55s T1 An inclined plank channel with riffle bars across the floor. Wash crushed material down it and the current carries the light waste away while the heavy fraction drops and lodges behind the riffles. It lets running water do the sorting your hands used to. sluice_trough_build_manual stone stair×1 cobblestone×8 lime mortar×2 → stone stair×1 Workbench 90s T2 Set stone steps in mortar: heavy and slow, but fireproof and effectively permanent. bld_build_stair_stone stamp mill (manual trip hammer)×1 construction wood×1 fieldstone×1 rope×1 → stamp mill (manual trip hammer)×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_stamp_mill_manual_trip_hammer_workbench tailings box×1 construction wood×6 → tailings box×1 Workbench station=true,station_input=1,station_output=1 • Station: workbench itemdb_tailings_box_workbench tailpole (windmill yaw)×1 construction wood×2 → tailpole (windmill yaw)×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_tailpole_windmill_yaw_workbench plant thread×1 plant fibers×2 → plant thread×1 Workbench 60s T1 170 kJ Spin retted plant fibres into a fine, strong thread. tex_spin_plant_thread treadle×1 rough board plank×2 wooden shaft (round)×1 wooden peg×3 rope×2 → treadle×1 Workbench 45s T1 A foot pedal linked by a pitman to a crank. It turns the weight of your leg into rotary power and frees both hands — the drive behind pole-lathes, looms, and grindstones. The first power source that is not somebody else's arms. treadle_build_manual brick wall×1 fired clay brick×10 cement mortar×3 → brick wall×1 Workbench 90s T3 Lay fired brick in mortar into a load-bearing wall that can carry a floor or roof directly. bld_build_wall_brick concrete wall×1 concrete block (CMU)×6 cement mortar×2 steel rebar×1 → concrete wall×1 Workbench 100s T3 240 kJ Stack concrete masonry units with mortar and pin them with rebar. Faster than poured wall forms, but still a modern cement-chain product. audit_cmu_to_concrete_wall concrete wall×1 wet concrete×4 steel rebar×1 → concrete wall×1 Workbench 90s T4 Pour a concrete wall around light rebar: a dense, weatherproof shell that doubles as structure. bld_build_wall_concrete wattle-and-daub wall×1 hazel rod×6 packed earth block×4 grass bundle×2 raw water×1 → wattle-and-daub wall×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_wall_wattle_and_daub_workbench waterwheel (overshot)×1 construction wood×1 rope×1 fieldstone×1 → waterwheel (overshot)×1 Workbench Optional late-T1 • Station: workbench itemdb_waterwheel_overshot_workbench waterwheel (undershot)×1 construction wood×6 rope×3 fieldstone×2 → waterwheel (undershot)×1 Workbench Optional late-T1 • Station: workbench itemdb_waterwheel_undershot_workbench wheel-and-axle×1 wooden gear (peg-toothed)×1 wooden shaft (round)×1 plain bearing (wood)×2 iron strap×1 → wheel-and-axle×1 Workbench 50s T1 A large wheel keyed to a thin axle on wooden bearings. A light pull on the rim becomes a strong turn at the core — the same trick as a windlass, but continuous. It is the heart of every geared machine you will build after this. wheel_and_axle_build_manual windlass×1 wooden shaft (round)×1 rough timber beam×2 forged iron crank×1 plain bearing (wood)×2 rope×2 → windlass×1 Workbench 65s T1 A horizontal drum wound by a forged iron crank turning in wooden bearings. The crank's leverage turns a weak, steady arm into a controlled lift — the standard way to raise water, ore, or a bucket from a shaft. windlass_build_manual wooden dowel×1 construction wood×1 → wooden dowel×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_wooden_dowel_workbench wooden gear (peg-toothed)×1 wooden dowel×1 construction wood×1 → wooden gear (peg-toothed)×1 Workbench Station: workbench itemdb_wooden_gear_peg_toothed_workbench wooden tub×1 rough board plank×6 rope×3 wooden peg×4 → wooden tub×1 Workbench 55s T1 Fit split planks into a ring of staves and bind them with rope hoops until the joints swell tight. It holds water, mash, dye, or hide-soak — the big open vessel a camp industry runs on. Slow to build because every stave has to be shaped to close the circle. wooden_tub_build_manual wool roving×1 washed wool×1 → wool roving×1 Workbench 45s T1 180 kJ Comb washed wool so the fibres run parallel, drawing it into a soft roving sliver. tex_card_wool wool yarn×1 wool roving×1 → wool yarn×1 Workbench 75s T1 180 kJ Draw and twist the roving into a strong continuous wool yarn on the spindle. tex_spin_wool_yarn

docs.title: Plain-English glossary
docs.text:
Conduvia's crafting tree is really a tour of how people actually make things. This page explains the real trick behind each big jump on the climb — in plain words, in one place. We keep the real names (they're worth knowing!), but every one comes with a "here's what that actually means" right next to it. Where we simplify something for the game, we say so.

Honest by design

We speed up the timing and round off the amounts so it's fun to play. The way each thing works is the real way.

docs.title: Heat & carbon
docs.text:
Charcoal. Heat wood in a pile with almost no air. Instead of burning up, the wood cooks: the smoke and steam get driven off, leaving behind nearly pure carbon. Charcoal burns much hotter and cleaner than plain wood — hot enough to melt metal. (The "cook it with no air" trick has a name: pyrolysis.)

Coke. The same trick, but on coal instead of wood. Bake coal with no air and the tar and gas cook off, leaving a light, super-hot fuel called coke. It burns hot enough — and stays solid enough — to hold up a tall furnace packed full of ore.

Quicklime. Roast limestone (the white rock, also called calcium carbonate) and it puffs out a gas (carbon dioxide), leaving quicklime behind. Quicklime helps metal melting go smoothly, and it's the starting point for mortar — the paste that holds bricks together.

docs.title: Metals
docs.text:
Bronze. Melt copper, then stir in a little tin. The mix is harder than either metal alone and melts at a lower heat — so handy that a whole age is named after it. (Mixing metals like this makes an alloy.)

Wrought iron. A short stone furnace called a bloomery pulls iron out of ore without fully melting it. You're left with a hot, spongy lump of iron mixed with glassy waste, which you hammer over and over to squeeze the waste out. The result is soft, tough iron you can shape — wrought just means "worked."

Steel. A tall blast furnace melts iron together with coke and a bit of rock helper into a high-carbon iron. Carbon is what makes iron hard but also brittle — so you carefully burn some of it back out. Land in the sweet spot and you get steel: the strong, springy metal the modern world is built from.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
Steam power. Burn fuel to boil water. The steam pushes hard as it expands, and that push shoves a piston or spins a wheel. Suddenly you have a worker that never gets tired — the engine that kicked off the factory age.

Generators (dynamos) and the grid. Spin a coil of wire near a magnet and you make electricity — that's a generator. A simple one (a DC dynamo) gets you started. A fancier kind (AC) can send power over long wires without wasting much, and run big motors. That's the moment electricity stops being a toy and starts running real factories.

docs.title: Electricity does chemistry (the Electric tier)
docs.text:
Aluminum. Aluminum clings to oxygen so tightly that fire can't pull them apart. Electricity can. You dissolve aluminum's powdery ore in a hot melted bath and push a huge current through it; pure aluminum collects at the bottom. People call this the Hall–Héroult process (named after its two inventors). Aluminum is basically electricity turned into metal — impossible before the power grid.

Chlor-alkali. Run electricity through salty water and it splits into three useful things at once: chlorine gas, hydrogen gas, and a strong cleaner/base called lye (sodium hydroxide). Tons of other chemistry starts from these three.

Ferroalloys and raw silicon. In a furnace heated by an electric arc (think lightning on tap), you roast quartz rock with carbon. The carbon steals the oxygen out of the rock and leaves behind about 98%-pure silicon — the seed of everything electronic. Doing it with carbon and heat like this is called carbothermic reduction (carbo = carbon, thermic = heat, reduction = pulling the oxygen off).

docs.title: Computer chips (the Solid State tier)
docs.text:
Super-pure silicon. That 98% silicon isn't nearly clean enough for chips. So you turn it into a gas, boil that gas over and over to scrub out the junk (like distilling), then turn it back into solid silicon that's something like a billion times purer. This clean-up is the Siemens process, and the result is polysilicon.

Growing a crystal wafer. Dip a tiny seed crystal into a pot of melted silicon and slowly pull it upward while spinning. The silicon freezes onto the seed in one flawless crystal, growing into a long shiny rod. Slice the rod into thin rounds — wafers — and you've got the blank discs every computer chip is printed on. This pulling trick is the Czochralski method.

docs.title: Space (the win)
docs.text:
Cold-trapping oxygen from air. Squeeze and chill air until it turns to liquid, then warm it back up bit by bit. Different gases boil off at different temperatures, so they separate — letting you collect pure liquid oxygen. That super-cold liquid oxygen is what your rocket breathes to burn its fuel. (Anything that cold is called cryogenic.)

Titanium. Titanium is light, super strong, and shrugs off heat — perfect for rockets — but it's a pain to make. You react its ore-gas with melted magnesium, which rips the metal free as a crumbly "sponge" you then melt down. This is the Kroll process.

Heat-proof metal mixes. A rocket engine has to survive its own fire. So you build it from special metal blends: tough nickel ones (like Inconel) for the pumps, and a copper-chromium mix for the chamber walls that get cooled from behind. Bolt on lightweight fuel tanks, fill them with chilled oxygen and rocket kerosene, stack it into a rocket — and launch.

docs.title: How this manual is compiled
docs.text:
This field manual is compiled directly from the physical and chemical laws governing the world, then hand-annotated. The automated systems lay out the raw industrial capabilities available to you; the handwritten notes provide the critical engineering context (formulas, diagrams, warnings) needed to survive them.

Archival Blueprints vs. Field Reality

The published manual reflects the current understanding of the world (1,247 items · 1,530 processes · 192 stations). However, survival is chaotic. Treat automated readouts as a foundation; your handwritten notes and chemical formulas are what will actually keep the factory running. Always verify your chemical assumptions against the raw materials in front of you.

docs.title: Data Extraction
docs.text:
Environmental Sensors & Physics Engine
   QuestBook/Content/Chapters/         (field logs)
   ItemDatabase/Data/                  (material properties)
   Stations/                           (machine schematics)
        |
        |  tools/lualit.py   (tolerant Lua-literal reader, no Lua runtime)
        |  tools/extract.py  ->  data/{quests,items,stations}.json
        v
   tools/gen_pages.py  ->  docs/  (the climb, field guides, stations, items, home)
        |
        v
   mkdocs build  ->  site/
  • tools/lualit.py parses Lua table literals directly in Python — strings, long-brackets, comments, computed keys, trailing commas, type casts, and string concatenation — so no Lua interpreter is needed to read the data.
  • tools/extract.py walks the chapters, item database, and station defs and emits clean JSON.
  • tools/gen_pages.py turns that JSON into the markdown you’re reading, plus the icon manifest.json.

docs.title: What’s hand-written
docs.text: The onboarding (Getting Started) and these Reference pages are written by hand — they’re explanation, not data. The pages under The Climb, Field Guides, Stations, and Items & Ores are scaffolded by the generator and then hand-augmented — the field-guide chemistry, the item-table Formula column, and the narrative notes are added on top of the generated structure and are not produced by gen_pages.py alone.

docs.title: Regenerating
docs.text:
python tools/extract.py --code /path/to/Conduvia/Code --out data
CONDUVIA_DATA=data CONDUVIA_DOCS=docs python tools/gen_pages.py
mkdocs build

docs.title: Custom components
docs.text: The look comes from docs/assets/css/conduvia.css (the field-manual design system) and tiers.css (per-tier accents). The :ci[item_id] item chips and :icon[item_id] glyphs are expanded by a native MkDocs hook, hooks/shortcodes.py — no third-party plugin required.

docs.title: Card & badge legend
docs.text: A quick key to the symbols used throughout this manual.

docs.title: Quest badges
docs.text: Badge Meaning Win-path On the critical line to orbit. Do these. Checkpoint Closes out a chapter / unlocks the next tier. Branch Optional. Quality-of-life, comfort, or a side-system. Briefing Read-only intro or explainer, no crafting. Exchange Token trade — upgrades and bundles.

docs.title: Quest card anatomy
docs.text:
Each quest card shows, top to bottom:

  • the badge and title;
  • Unlocks after — the quests you must finish first;
  • a short “what do I do” summary in the game’s own voice;
  • Do this — the concrete tasks, each with a kind tag (craft, retrieve, place …), what it needs (inputs) and what it yields (outputs);
  • Rewards (and Costs, for exchanges);
  • a collapsible Background with the real-world context.

docs.title: Item chips
docs.text: Items appear as chips: rope is an item, and plant fibers×10 is an item with a count (here, ten). The little square is the item’s icon — or a category-tinted monogram until its art is finished.

docs.title: Station slots
docs.text: in ×N input slots · fuel ×N fuel slots · out ×N output slots · no panel works just by being placed.

docs.title: Tier colours
docs.text: Each tier owns an accent colour, used on its chapter page, rungs, and cards: Survival (moss), Stone (ash), Metal Ages (copper), Steam (brass), Steel & DC (gunmetal/amber), Electric (arc-blue), Solid State (violet), Space (indigo).

docs.title: Stations
docs.text:
Stations are the machines and work surfaces you craft at. Each one is modeled on a piece of real-world equipment. Drop a station from your inventory to place it, then open it to queue recipes. Stations marked passive have no crafting panel — they work or monitor automatically once placed.

Absorption Tower absorption_tower passive

SO3 gas is absorbed into circulating concentrated sulfuric acid in an acid-proof packed tower to make the final acid/oleum. Steel shell, ceramic packing, acid piping.

Crafted at machine shop (electric).

AC District Network network_ac_district in ×1 out ×2

Gathers the power from several generators and spreads it across a whole area — a hub where the wires meet before fanning out to the buildings around it.

Can't be opened — it just shows the network's state.

AC Grid Mimic Panel panel_mimic_ac_grid in ×1 out ×2

A board that shows your whole power grid at a glance — how much each generator is making, which switches are on or off, and where something has gone wrong. (A status board like this is called a mimic panel.)

Just for reading — there's nothing to click.

AC Induction Motor motor_ac_induction_small in ×1 out ×2

Plug it into back-and-forth electricity and it just spins — no contacts rubbing or wearing out, so it's tough and nearly maintenance-free. (Back-and-forth current is called AC, and this kind of motor is an induction motor.)

Needs an AC supply at the right frequency.

Refinery heart: a reboiled tray column splits desalted crude by boiling range into naphtha, kerosene, gasoil and heavy bottoms. This is separation, not magic fuel-making.

Petroleum stage 3 - fractionation: desalted crude + heat/power -> naphtha, kerosene, gasoil and residuum.

Pump this air bag by hand to blast air into a fire. More air makes the fuel burn hotter — hot enough to work metal a plain fire can't touch. Set it next to a forge and it speeds up the heat.

Runs a little electricity through a thin carbon thread until it glows warm amber. It's one of the first light bulbs — pretty, but fragile and quick to burn out. (A bulb that lights up by heating a thread like this is called incandescent.)

Screw it into a lamp fixture; swap it out when it burns out.

A part, not a machine. This is the iron box where the fire burns inside a boiler. Cast it at the Clay Casting Pit first, then use it as one of the pieces when you build the Riveted Boiler.

A part used to build the Riveted Boiler.

A field of microwave antennas and fast rectifiers tied into a protected DC bus. It represents the receiver side of an orbital solar-power system after the SPS/beamer package exists.

Wire the DC output into a compatible grid or battery. If there is no demand, the Inspector will show the source as idle — not broken.

The contact process passes SO2 + air over vanadium-pentoxide catalyst beds to make SO3. Steel vessel with stacked catalyst trays and interbed cooling.

The Peirce-Smith converter blows air through tuyeres into molten copper matte, oxidizing iron and sulfur to leave blister copper. Refractory-lined steel barrel that tilts.

Crafted at machine shop (steam).

Refinery front-end: hot-water/caustic washing and settling remove brine, grit and metal salts before distillation. Salty crude corrodes columns; desalting is not optional.

Petroleum stage 2 - crude conditioning: raw crude + water + caustic + AC power -> desalted crude.

Impure copper anodes dissolve and pure copper plates onto cathodes in an acid sulfate bath under DC. Lined tank, copper bus bars, step-down transformer.

A part, not a machine. A pump that pushes the recovered water back into the boiler so it never runs dry. Used when building the Riveted Boiler.

A part used to build the Riveted Boiler.

Blister copper is fire-refined by blowing air then reducing with gas to remove oxygen, then cast into anodes. Refractory-lined steel furnace with tuyeres.

Crafted at machine shop (steam).

Firewood Rack storage_firewood_rack in ×1

Stack split wood on this rack to keep it up off the wet ground. Air moves around it and dries it out faster, so it burns better and doesn't rot.

Shift-click firewood from your inventory to store it quickly.

A pipe fitting that splits, joins, and steers liquids and gases between machines. A valve sets how much gets through, and a gauge shows what's flowing and how fast.

Inspect it to see the flow rate and which fluid is moving.

Fluoride Digestion Reactor fluoride_digestion_reactor in ×4 out ×2

Fluorine Cell fluorine_cell in ×4 out ×2

Flywheel flywheel passive

Francis Water Turbine water_turbine_francis in ×1 out ×1

Water under head from a penstock enters the spiral scroll case, spins the enclosed runner, and drains down the draft tube. The shaft delivers steady baseload power to a generator day and night, as long as the water keeps flowing.

Feed it penstock water; couple its shaft to a generator.

Froth Flotation Cell froth_flotation_cell passive

Reagents make target minerals water-repellent so they cling to air bubbles and float into a froth that overflows, leaving gangue behind. Stirred, aerated steel cell.

Crafted at machine shop (electric).

Fuel Rod Assembly Line fuel_rod_assembly_line in ×4 out ×2

Squeezes a gas into a much smaller space, packing it under high pressure so it can be piped onward or stored. A spinning shaft drives the piston that does the squeezing.

Sends pressurized gas on to the next machine.

Gas Generator Set genset_gas_engine in ×1 out ×1

A gas engine bolted to an alternator. Load raw natural gas into the input slot and it burns it to put AC onto the line on demand, venting CO2 to the output. It only supplies power while it is running and fuelled — your dispatchable backup for when the wind drops and the sun is down.

Load natural gas to run; it feeds AC to the wired network.

Geared Gristmill gristmill_geared in ×2 out ×2

Ground Station Dish ground_station_dish in ×1 out ×1

A powered S-band ground station: steerable dish, low-noise amplifier, transceiver and control computer. It is the real ground endpoint for satellite telemetry and command uplink.

Feed 480 V AC. If the Inspector says no live source or below-voltage, fix the electrical grid before blaming the satellite chain.

Ground Tracking Radar tracking_radar_ground in ×1 out ×1

A powered tracking radar for launch and early-orbit checkout. It measures range/bearing so the pad can prove a vehicle actually reached the intended trajectory envelope.

A powered microwave relay hut with dish, mast, battery buffer and alarm. High ground matters: real microwave links need line-of-sight paths, not magic global chat bubbles.

Place on high ground and feed AC power. It extends the visible satellite/telemetry network.

Hot Blast Stove hot_blast_stove in ×1 out ×2

Burns the blast furnace's own waste gas to heat a tall stack of firebrick red-hot. Then the draft is switched: cold air is blown through the hot brick and comes out scorching. Feeding the furnace hot air instead of cold lets it run far hotter on much less fuel. This isn't a crafting station — it's a helper that makes the furnace next to it work better. (It stores heat in brick and hands it back to the air — a regenerative, or 'Cowper', stove.)

Place it next to a Blast Furnace to preheat its air blast.

A hanging lamp that throws bright light down over a work area so you can see what you're doing after dark. Holds either a glowing-thread bulb or a brighter arc lamp.

Needs power on the circuit to light up.

Iron Belt Pulley belt_pulley_iron passive

A part, not a machine. It cools the used-up steam leaving an engine and turns it back into water, so that water can be boiled again instead of wasted — which saves fuel. Used when building the Riveted Boiler. (Turning steam back into water is called condensing.)

A part used to build the Riveted Boiler.

Catalytic cleanup: hydrogen under pressure strips sulfur and unstable molecules from straight-run kerosene. The sulfur leaves as H2S for the Claus sulfur unit.

Sucks air out of a sealed space until there's almost nothing left inside — a vacuum. That low pressure helps you filter liquids, boil things at lower heat, and seal glass tubes.

A tall wooden pole that holds electric wires up in the air and out of the way. Line up a row of them to carry power across your base — the simplest way to move electricity around.

Reverberatory Furnace reverberatory_furnace passive
